title: Arakawa–Suzuki Functors and Higher-Level Schur–Weyl Duality

items.title: The degenerate affine Hecke algebra
items.statement:
Work over the field $\mathbb C$ and fix an integer $d\ge 0$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[def-commutative-ring]]). Let
$\mathcal F_d$ be the free associative unital $\mathbb C$-algebra on the
$d+\max(d-1,0)$ symbols $x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ (for $d=0$ there is only
the unit; for $d=1$ only $x_1$), with its word basis and universal property
([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]), and let
$I_d\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}\mathcal F_d$ be the two-sided ideal
([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]], [[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]])
generated by the following elements:

- $x_ix_j-x_jx_i$ for all $1\le i,j\le d$;
- $s_i^2-1$, $s_is_{i+1}s_i-s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1}$, and $s_is_j-s_js_i$ for
  $|i-j|>1$, for $1\le i,j\le d-1$;
- $s_ix_j-x_js_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$, $s_ix_{i+1}-x_is_i-1$, and
  $x_{i+1}s_i-s_ix_i-1$, for $1\le i\le d-1$ and $1\le j\le d$.

The **degenerate affine Hecke algebra** is the quotient $\mathbb C$-algebra
$$H_d:=\mathcal F_d/I_d$$
with unit element written $1$ ([[thm-quotient-ring-laws]]). We keep the symbols
$x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ for their images, and for $w\in S_d$ we write
$w$ for the image in $H_d$ of any word in the $s_i$ representing $w$; this is
independent of the chosen word once the basis theorem below is proved. For
$d\ge1$ and $a\in\mathbb C$, the notation $H_d/(x_1-a)$ means the quotient by the two-sided
ideal generated by $x_1-a$.

The verification below establishes exactly the structure of $H_d$ used
throughout this page: the ordered monomials
$$x_1^{r_1}\cdots x_d^{r_d}w,\qquad r_1,\dots,r_d\ge0,\ w\in S_d,$$
form a $\mathbb C$-basis, so that
$H_d\cong\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C[S_d]$ as a vector
space with polynomial and group-algebra subalgebras
([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]], [[def-group-ring]]);
$H_0=\mathbb C$ and $H_1=\mathbb C[x_1]$; for $d\ge1$ and every $a$ there is a unique
algebra isomorphism
$$H_d/(x_1-a)\cong\mathbb C[S_d],\qquad x_j\longmapsto a+\sum_{k<j}(k\ j);$$
and total polynomial degree is an algebra filtration whose associated graded is
the semidirect product $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\rtimes\mathbb C[S_d]$ in which
$s_i$ acts by swapping $x_i$ and $x_{i+1}$. For $d\ge2$, the cross relation is
inhomogeneous, so it does not turn $H_d$ into a graded algebra with
$\deg x_i=1$ and $\deg s_i=0$. For $d=0$ the algebra $\mathbb C$ has its
degree-zero grading, and for $d=1$ the algebra $\mathbb C[x_1]$ has its
natural polynomial grading.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The data of [F1]-[F6]: the presented algebra $H_d=\mathcal F_d/I_d$, the symmetric group $S_d$, the group algebra $\mathbb C[S_d]$, the polynomial algebra $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]$ with fraction field $\Omega$, and the tensor-product and quotient structures.

1.1 The cases $d=0,1$. For $d=0$ there are no symbols, so $\mathcal F_0=\mathbb C$ and $I_0=0$, giving $H_0=\mathbb C$. For $d=1$ the only symbol is $x_1$ and the list of relations is empty; the words in $x_1$ are $1,x_1,x_1^2,\dots$, a $\mathbb C$-basis of $\mathcal F_1$ by [F4], so $H_1$ is the polynomial algebra $\mathbb C[x_1]$ with basis $x_1^r$, $r\ge0$. [F3, F4, given]

1.2 The rational-function model. On the $\mathbb C$-vector space $\Omega$ of [F3] let $m_f$ denote multiplication by $f\in\Omega$, and for $1\le i<d$ let $\sigma_i$ be the operator $(\sigma_if)(y_1,\dots,y_d)=f(y_1,\dots,y_{i+1},y_i,\dots,y_d)$ interchanging the $i$-th and $(i+1)$-st arguments. Put $a_i:=d_i^{-1}\in\Omega$ (invertible by [F3]), $\delta_i:=a_i(1+\sigma_i)$ and $T_i:=\sigma_i-\delta_i$. For a word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$ in the generators of $S_d$ set $\sigma_w:=\sigma_{i_1}\!\circ\cdots\circ\sigma_{i_k}$ and $T_w:=T_{i_1}\!\cdots T_{i_k}$. The operators $\sigma_w$ are well defined by the Coxeter presentation [F1], because the $\sigma_i$ satisfy those relations and the presentation says that any two words for the same $w$ are related by them. [F1, F3, construct]

1.3 The skew algebra. Let $D:=\{\sum_{w\in S_d}m_{f_w}\sigma_w:f_w\in\Omega\}\subseteq\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\Omega)$, a $\mathbb C$-subspace. For $f,g\in\Omega$ and $u,v\in S_d$ the identities $\sigma_um_g=m_{\sigma_u(g)}\sigma_u$ and $\sigma_u\sigma_v=\sigma_{uv}$ hold (the first expresses the substitution action on functions, the second is word concatenation), so $(m_f\sigma_u)(m_g\sigma_v)=m_{f\,\sigma_u(g)}\sigma_{uv}$; hence $D$ is a subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\Omega)$. The set $\{\sigma_w\}$ is $\Omega$-linearly independent: suppose $\sum_wf_w\sigma_w=0$ with $f_w\in\Omega$ not all zero; multiplying the resulting identity of functions by a common denominator of the $f_w$, we may assume $f_w\in\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]$. Fix integers $N_1>\cdots>N_d$ whose consecutive gaps exceed the total degree of every $f_w$, and order the finitely many $w$ with $f_w\ne0$ by the lexicographic order of the vectors $w\cdot N:=(N_{w^{-1}(1)},\dots,N_{w^{-1}(d)})$; let $w$ be maximal and let $e$ be the exponent of a top monomial of $f_w$. Applying the sum to the monomial $y^N$ gives $\sum_{w'}f_{w'}(y)\,y^{w'\cdot N}$, because $\sigma_{w'}y^N=y^{w'\cdot N}$; the vectors $w'\cdot N$ are distinct, and at the first coordinate where $w'\cdot N$ differs from $w\cdot N$ the gap exceeds the degree bound, so the monomial $y^{w\cdot N+e}$ occurs exactly once, in the summand $f_wy^{w\cdot N}$, with nonzero coefficient. This contradicts the vanishing of the sum, proving the claim. [F3, algebra, given]

1.4 Spanning of $H_d$ by ordered monomials. We show that every element of $H_d$ is a $\mathbb C$-linear combination of the images of ordered monomials $x^rw$; since words span $\mathcal F_d$ by [F4], it suffices to treat the image of a word $W$ in the symbols. Use strong induction on the pair $(n,\iota)$ ordered lexicographically, where $n$ is the number of $x$-symbols in $W$ and $\iota$ is the number of pairs of positions $(p<q)$ such that the $p$-th symbol is some $s_i$ and the $q$-th symbol is some $x_j$. If $n=0$, then $W$ is a word in the $s_i$; by the Coxeter presentation [F1] the subalgebra generated by the $s_i$ is spanned by the images of the elements $w\in S_d$, so the claim holds. If $n>0$ and every $x$-symbol precedes every $s$-symbol in $W$, then $W$ is of the form (word in $x$'s)(word in $s$'s), and the claim follows from commutativity of the $x$'s and the case $n=0$. Otherwise $W=W_1s_ix_jW_2$ with adjacent symbols; use $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i+1$ if $j=i+1$, $s_ix_i=x_{i+1}s_i-1$ if $j=i$ (the relation $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i+1$ solved for $s_ix_i$), and $s_ix_j=x_js_i$ if $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$. In every case $W\equiv W_1x_{j'}s_iW_2\pm W_1W_2$, where the first word has the same $n$ and one fewer $(s,x)$-inversion pair, while the second has $n-1$ $x$-symbols; both fall under the induction hypothesis. Hence the images of ordered monomials span $H_d$. [F1, F3, F4, given, construct]

1.5 Jucys-Murphy elements. For $1\le j\le d$ put $J_j:=\sum_{k<j}(k\ j)\in\mathbb C[S_d]$, so $J_1=0$. Then (i) $J_iJ_j=J_jJ_i$ for all $i,j$; (ii) $s_iJ_j=J_js_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$; and (iii) $s_iJ_{i+1}=J_is_i+1$. For (i) with $i<j$ write $\Omega_m:=\sum_{1\le k<l\le m}(k\ l)$ for the sum of all transpositions in $S_m$; $\Omega_m$ is central in $\mathbb C[S_m]$ because conjugation permutes the transpositions, and $J_m=\Omega_m-\Omega_{m-1}$. Since $J_i\in\mathbb C[S_i]\subseteq\mathbb C[S_{m-1}]\subset\mathbb C[S_m]$ for $i<m$, centrality of $\Omega_m$ in $\mathbb C[S_m]$ and of $\Omega_{m-1}$ in $\mathbb C[S_{m-1}]$ gives $[J_i,J_m]=[J_i,\Omega_m]-[J_i,\Omega_{m-1}]=0$. For (ii), conjugation by $s_i$ sends each transposition $(k\ j)$ to $(s_i(k)\ s_i(j))$; if $j<i$ both entries are fixed, and if $j>i+1$ the sum over $k<j$ contains the pairs with $k=i$ and $k=i+1$, whose images are interchanged, so the sum is preserved. For (iii), conjugation sends $(k\ i+1)$ to $(k\ i)$ for $k<i$ and fixes $(i\ i+1)$, so $s_iJ_{i+1}s_i=J_i+s_i$; multiplying on the right by $s_i$ and using $s_i^2=1$ gives (iii). [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The model satisfies the relations. Since $\sigma_im_{a_i}=m_{\sigma_i(a_i)}\sigma_i=m_{-a_i}\sigma_i$, the operator identity $(1+\sigma_i)m_{a_i}=m_{a_i}(1-\sigma_i)$ and the rules $\sigma_i\delta_i=-\delta_i$, $\delta_i\sigma_i=\delta_i$ hold; hence $\delta_i^2=m_{a_i}(1+\sigma_i)m_{a_i}(1+\sigma_i)=m_{a_i^2}(1-\sigma_i)(1+\sigma_i)=0$ and $T_i^2=\sigma_i^2-\sigma_i\delta_i-\delta_i\sigma_i+\delta_i^2=1+\delta_i-\delta_i+0=1$. For $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$ both $\sigma_i$ and $\delta_i$ commute with $m_{x_j}$, so $T_im_{x_j}=m_{x_j}T_i$. For the cross relations, use $\sigma_im_{x_{i+1}}=m_{x_i}\sigma_i$, $\sigma_im_{x_i}=m_{x_{i+1}}\sigma_i$ and the two identities $m_{x_i}\delta_i-\delta_im_{x_{i+1}}=1$ and $\delta_im_{x_i}-m_{x_{i+1}}\delta_i=1$: for the first, $m_{x_i}\delta_i=m_{a_ix_i}(1+\sigma_i)$ while $\delta_im_{x_{i+1}}=m_{a_ix_{i+1}}+m_{a_ix_i}\sigma_i$, and their difference is $m_{a_i(x_i-x_{i+1})}=1$; the second is the same computation with the roles of $x_i$ and $x_{i+1}$ interchanged. Therefore $T_im_{x_{i+1}}-m_{x_i}T_i=(m_{x_i}\sigma_i-m_{x_i}\sigma_i)+(m_{x_i}\delta_i-\delta_im_{x_{i+1}})=1$ and $m_{x_{i+1}}T_i-T_im_{x_i}=1$. For $|i-j|>1$, the variables and swaps in $T_i,T_j$ are disjoint, so they commute. For the braid relation put $A=(x_i-x_{i+1})^{-1}$, $B=(x_{i+1}-x_{i+2})^{-1}$, $C=(x_i-x_{i+2})^{-1}$, so $AB=C(A+B)$. The product rule of step 1.3 expands both $T_iT_{i+1}T_i$ and $T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}$ with coefficients, in the order $1,\sigma_i,\sigma_{i+1},\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1},\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i,\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i$, equal to $(-C(1+AB),BC(1-A),AC(1-B),-B(1-A)(1-C),-A(1-B)(1-C),(1-A)(1-B)(1-C))$. Here $A(B-C)=BC$ and $B(A-C)=AC$, both consequences of $AB=C(A+B)$, give the two shorter-swap coefficients and the common identity coefficient. Thus the braid relation holds. Hence the assignment $x_i\mapsto m_{x_i}$, $s_i\mapsto T_i$ preserves all the relations of the Definition, and by the universal properties [F4] it defines an algebra homomorphism $\Phi\colon H_d\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\Omega)$. [F1, F4, algebra]

2.2 Triangular expansion. Fix $w\in S_d$ with a reduced word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$, and put $c:=\prod_{t=1}^k(\sigma_{i_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_{t-1}})(1-a_{i_t})\ne0$ in $\Omega$, with the empty prefix acting as the identity. Every transported factor is nonzero because the prefix is a field automorphism. In the expansion of $T_w=\prod_t\bigl((1-a_{i_t})\sigma_{i_t}-a_{i_t}\bigr)$ by the product rule of step 1.3, the term choosing the factor $(1-a_{i_t})\sigma_{i_t}$ for every $t$ contributes $c\,\sigma_w$ after the scalar coefficients are moved left, while every other term is $m_g\sigma_v$ with $v$ the product of a proper subword of $s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$ in the induced order. If $\ell$ denotes the minimal number of generators needed to express a permutation, then such a proper subword $J$ has $\ell(v)\le|J|<k=\ell(w)$, using subadditivity of $\ell$ and reducedness. Collecting the expansion in the $\Omega$-basis $\{\sigma_v\}$ therefore gives $T_w=c\,\sigma_w+\sum_{\ell(v)<\ell(w)}c_v\sigma_v$ with $c\ne0$ and $c_v\in\Omega$. [F1, step 1.3, algebra]

2.3 The evaluation homomorphism. Assume $d\ge1$. The assignment $x_j\mapsto a+J_j$, $s_i\mapsto s_i$ defines an algebra homomorphism $\varphi\colon\mathcal F_d\to\mathbb C[S_d]$: the images of the $x$'s commute by step 1.5(i); the images of the $s_i$ satisfy the Coxeter relations by [F1]; and the cross relations follow from step 1.5(ii) and from $s_i(a+J_{i+1})=(a+J_i)s_i+1$, $(a+J_{i+1})s_i=s_i(a+J_i)+1$, which are step 1.5(iii) read in both directions. Since $\varphi(x_1-a)=a+J_1-a=0$, the quotient universal property [F4] yields an algebra homomorphism $\bar\varphi\colon H_d/(x_1-a)\to\mathbb C[S_d]$, which is surjective because the $s_i$ generate $S_d$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.5, construct]

3.1 Independence of the monomials in the model. By step 2.2 the change-of-basis matrix from $\{T_w\}$ to $\{\sigma_w\}$ inside $D$ is triangular with nonzero diagonal when permutations are ordered by length, hence invertible over the field $\Omega$; thus $\{T_w:w\in S_d\}$ is an $\Omega$-basis of $D$. Suppose $\sum_{r,w}c_{r,w}m_{x^r}T_w=0$ in $D$ with $c_{r,w}\in\mathbb C$ finitely supported. Grouping by $w$ gives $\sum_wP_wT_w=0$ with $P_w=\sum_rc_{r,w}x^r\in\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\subseteq\Omega$; $\Omega$-independence of the $T_w$ forces $P_w=0$ for every $w$, and linear independence of the monomials [F3] then forces $c_{r,w}=0$. Hence the elements $\Phi(x_1^{r_1}\cdots x_d^{r_d}w)$ are $\mathbb C$-linearly independent. [F3, step 1.3, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Basis theorem. Let $h\in H_d$ and write $h=\sum c_{r,w}x^rw$ using step 1.4. If $h=0$, applying the homomorphism $\Phi$ of step 2.1 gives $\sum c_{r,w}m_{x^r}T_w=0$, and step 3.1 yields $c_{r,w}=0$. Hence the ordered monomials form a $\mathbb C$-basis of $H_d$, and the $\mathbb C$-linear map $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C[S_d]\to H_d$, $f\otimes w\mapsto fw$, is an isomorphism by [F5]; in particular $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]$ and $\mathbb C[S_d]$ are subalgebras of $H_d$ and the cross relations hold. The elementary cases $H_0=\mathbb C$, $H_1=\mathbb C[x_1]$ were recorded in step 1.1. [F2, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.4]

5.1 The inverse map. Assume $d\ge1$. In $H_d$ the relation $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i+1$ gives, after left multiplication by $s_i$ and use of $s_i^2=1$, the recursion $x_{i+1}=s_ix_is_i+s_i$. Hence in $H_d/(x_1-a)$ one has $x_1\equiv a$ and inductively $x_j\equiv a+u_j$ with $u_j$ in the subalgebra generated by the images of the $s_i$, namely $u_1=0$ and $u_{j+1}=s_ju_js_j+s_j$. By the basis theorem of step 4.1 every element of $H_d$ is a combination of monomials $x^rw$, and replacing each $x_j$ by $a+u_j$ expresses its image in $H_d/(x_1-a)$ as an element of the image of the subalgebra generated by the $s_i$; by [F1] and [F2] that image is the $\mathbb C$-span of $\{w:w\in S_d\}$. Therefore the canonical map $\rho\colon\mathbb C[S_d]\to H_d/(x_1-a)$, $w\mapsto w+(x_1-a)$, has image equal to the whole quotient, and it is injective because $\bar\varphi\circ\rho=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C[S_d]}$ by construction; hence $\rho$ is an isomorphism. Under it $x_j$ corresponds to $a+u_j$, and $\bar\varphi(a+u_j)=a+J_j$ by step 2.3, so $\bar\varphi(x_j)=a+\sum_{k<j}(k\ j)$; in particular $x_1$ corresponds to the scalar $a$, while for $j\ge2$ the image is not the scalar $a$. [F1, F2, step 4.1, step 2.3, algebra]

5.2 The degree filtration. For $k\ge0$ let $F_k\subseteq H_d$ be the image of the $\mathbb C$-span of all words in the symbols containing at most $k$ of the symbols $x_1,\dots,x_d$. Steps 1.4 and 4.1 identify $F_k$ with the span of the monomials $x^rw$ with $|r|\le k$. The substitution rules of step 1.4 replace an adjacent pair $s_ix_j$ by terms containing at most one $x$-symbol each, so a product of a word with $k$ $x$-symbols and a word with $m$ $x$-symbols rewrites into words with at most $k+m$ $x$-symbols; hence $F_kF_m\subseteq F_{k+m}$ and $(F_k)_{k\ge0}$ is an algebra filtration with $1\in F_0$. [F4, step 1.4, step 4.1]

6.1 The associated graded is a semidirect product. Let $S:=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\rtimes\mathbb C[S_d]$ be the algebra with $\mathbb C$-basis $x^rw$ and product $x^rw\cdot x^{r'}w'=x^{r+w\cdot r'}ww'$, where $(w\cdot r')_j=r'_{w^{-1}(j)}$; equivalently, $S$ is generated by the symbols $x_i$ and $w$ subject to the relations obtained from those of $H_d$ by deleting the inhomogeneous term $1$ from both cross relations, i.e. $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i$ and $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i$. In $\mathrm{gr}\,H_d$ the defining relations of $H_d$ project to these relations: the commutativity, Coxeter and distant-commutation relations are homogeneous of the stated degrees, while the two cross relations have the form (degree $1$ element) $=1$ (degree $0$ element), so their degree-$1$ parts are exactly $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i$ and $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i$. Consequently there is a surjective graded algebra homomorphism $S\to\mathrm{gr}\,H_d$ sending $x_i$ and $w$ to the symbols of $x_i$ and $w$. In degree $k$ both sides are $\mathbb C$-spanned by the symbols $x^rw$ with $|r|=k$: these form a spanning set of $\mathrm{gr}_kH_d$ by step 5.2 together with the basis theorem of step 4.1, and they form the basis of the degree-$k$ part of $S$ by construction; a surjection between $\mathbb C$-vector spaces with a spanning set of the same finite cardinality as a basis of the target is an isomorphism. Hence $\mathrm{gr}\,H_d\cong S$ in every degree, and the associated graded is the semidirect product $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\rtimes\mathbb C[S_d]$ in which $s_i$ swaps $x_i$ and $x_{i+1}$, as claimed. [F2, F5, step 4.1, step 5.2, algebra]

7.1 Polynomial grading boundaries. For $d=0$, step 1.1 gives $H_0=\mathbb C$ with its degree-zero grading; for $d=1$, it gives $H_1=\mathbb C[x_1]$ with the usual polynomial grading. For $d\ge2$, suppose there were an algebra grading $H_d=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}H_d^{(k)}$ with $x_i$ in degree $1$ and $s_i$ in degree $0$. Then the relation $s_ix_{i+1}-x_is_i=1$ would have its left-hand side in degree $1$ and its right-hand side in degree $0$, forcing $1=0$, which is impossible. Hence for $d\ge2$ the polynomial-degree filtration of step 5.2 does not arise from that generator grading; its cross relation is inhomogeneous. [F6, step 1.1, step 5.2] ∎

items.title: Type-A nilpotent orbit closures are normal via chain varieties
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $e$ be a nilpotent endomorphism of a
finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$ ([[def-nilpotent-endomorphism]]),
let $X=\overline{\mathrm{GL}(V)\cdot e}$ be the closure in
$\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ of its conjugacy orbit
([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]), and let
$\partial X=X\setminus\mathrm{GL}(V)\cdot e$. Then $\mathbb C[X]$ is a reduced
irreducible normal domain and $\operatorname{codim}_X\partial X\ge2$. This
holds for every Jordan type, not only the regular nilpotent cone.

The proof uses the *chain schemes*: if the Jordan partition of $e$ has column
lengths $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_t>0$, put $n_i=q_t+\cdots+q_{t-i+1}$ and
$U_i=\mathbb C^{n_i}$ for $0\le i\le t$. Let $M=\prod_{i=1}^{t-1}\bigl(\operatorname{Hom}(U_i,U_{i+1})\times\operatorname{Hom}(U_{i+1},U_i)\bigr)$
with coordinates $(A_i,B_i)$ and let $Z\subseteq M$ be the closed subscheme
$B_1A_1=0$, $B_iA_i=A_{i-1}B_{i-1}$ $(2\le i<t)$. Then $Z$ is a complete
intersection, smooth outside a closed subset of codimension $\ge2$, reduced,
irreducible and normal, and the invariant ring $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ under
$H=\prod_{i<t}\mathrm{GL}(U_i)$ is the coordinate ring of $X$ via the end map
$\theta=A_{t-1}B_{t-1}$ when $t\ge2$. For the empty Jordan diagram ($V=0$,
$t=0$) and the single-column diagram ($e=0$, $t=1$), the chain has no
variables or equations: take $Z=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$, $H$ trivial
and $\theta=0$; the equation list above is imposed only on existing links.
In these cases $X$ is a point, its boundary is empty, and its boundary
codimension is $+\infty$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** AC, the nilpotent endomorphism $e$, its Jordan columns $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_t>0$, and the chain scheme and end map of the Statement, including its empty-chain conventions.

1.1 **Empty chains.** If $V=0$, take $t=0$; if $e=0$ on a nonzero space, its Jordan diagram has a single column and $t=1$. In either case there are no chain variables or equations, $Z=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C$, $H$ is trivial and $\theta=0$. Its image is the point orbit closure, its coordinate ring is a normal domain, and the empty equation sequence is regular. The boundary is empty and has codimension $+\infty$. All conclusions follow in these cases. Henceforth $t\ge2$. [given, algebra]

1.2 **The open chain locus.** Put $c=\sum_{i<t}n_i^2$ and $D=2\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}-c$. The differential of the chain equations is $Y_iA_i+B_iX_i-X_{i-1}B_{i-1}-A_{i-1}Y_{i-1}$, with the index-zero terms zero. If each $A_i$ is injective or $B_i$ is surjective, these equations can be solved successively for any prescribed right-hand sides: use a left inverse of $A_i$ to choose $Y_i$, or a right inverse of $B_i$ to choose $X_i$, after the preceding pair is fixed. Thus the open locus $Z^\circ$ with this condition is smooth of dimension $D$ by [F4]. It is nonempty: use $U_i=\operatorname{im}e^{t-i}$, inclusions $A_i$, and restrictions $B_i=e|_{U_{i+1}}$, transported to the fixed spaces. These maps satisfy the equations and have end map $e$. [F1, F3, F4, construct, algebra]

1.3 **Alternating strings and their stabilizers.** For a nilpotent pair $A:U\to W$, $B:W\to U$, the odd operator $T$ on $U\oplus W$ with these components has a homogeneous Jordan-string decomposition: kernels and images of its powers are graded, so the complements in the Jordan construction may be chosen homogeneous. Every string alternates letters $a$ from $U$ and $b$ from $W$. Removing all $b$ letters gives the Jordan rows of $BA$, and removing all $a$ letters gives those of $AB$. The ranks of alternating composites recover the numbers of strings of each length and starting letter, so a diagram determines one pair orbit and there are finitely many diagrams in fixed dimensions. The pair stabilizer is the unit group of its even endomorphism algebra, an open subset of a vector space and hence smooth and irreducible. On a string $A$ kills exactly a terminal $a$ and $B$ misses exactly an initial $a$; consequently $A$ is injective iff every string ends in $b$, and $B$ is surjective iff every string begins in $b$. [F1, F2, algebra, construct]

1.4 **Even orbit drops.** Distinct dominated types have strictly smaller orbit dimension. One can move from a dominating partition to a dominated one by repeatedly moving a box from an earlier row to a later allowable row: choose an excess row and a subsequent deficit row, taking the last row of the source plateau and the first allowed destination to preserve the partition inequalities, and repeat until the target is reached. A move from row $i$ to row $j>i$ increases $\sum_r(2r-1)\mu_r$ by $2(j-i)$ and therefore decreases the orbit dimension by that positive even number. Each allowable unit move from row lengths $a,b$ with $a\ge b+2$ is realized by a one-parameter degeneration. On chains $u_1,\ldots,u_{a-1}$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_{b+1}$ of the destination type, keep the usual lowering maps except send $v_{b+1}$ to $v_b+z u_{a-1}$, with $v_0=0$. At $z=0$ the type is $(a-1,b+1)$; for $z\ne0$ the ranks of powers are those of $(a,b)$ (the chain generated by $v_{b+1}$ has length $a$, and the remaining chain has length $b$). Keeping other strings fixed proves that dominated types belong to the top orbit closure. Hence a drop of exactly two consists of one box moved to the next row; any other drop is at least four. Equivalently, parity also follows from $\sum_j(\mu'_j)^2\equiv\sum_j\mu'_j=N\pmod2$ for the total sum; individual summands in a difference of square sums need not be even. [F3, algebra]

2.1 **The pair-orbit dimension.** Write $m=\dim U$, $n=\dim W$, and let $E,O$ be the dimensions of the even and odd centralizers of $T$. A homomorphism between Jordan strings of lengths $L,L'$ has $\min(L,L')$ possible shifts. Counting the parity of those shifts, odd strings of the same endpoint type contribute $+1$ to the even-minus-odd count, and odd strings of opposite type contribute $-1$; the two opposite Hom directions for an odd/even pair cancel, and even/even pairs contribute zero. Summing gives $E-O=(m-n)^2$, because the difference between the numbers of odd $a$-type and odd $b$-type strings is $m-n$. The pair orbit therefore has dimension $m^2+n^2-E=\tfrac12((m+n)^2-E-O)$, half the dimension of the ordinary orbit of $T$. If a string has $r_j$ letters $a$ and $s_j$ letters $b$, then $\min(r_j+s_j,r_k+s_k)=\min(r_j,r_k)+\min(s_j,s_k)$ except for equal odd lengths with opposite endpoint types, where the left side is larger by one. Let $a_l,b_l$ count the odd strings of length $l$ beginning with the two respective letters, and put $\Delta=\sum_{l\text{ odd}}a_lb_l$. The ordinary Jordan centralizer counts now give $\dim O_{(A,B)}=mn+\tfrac12(\dim C_{BA}+\dim C_{AB})-\Delta$. This is a dimension identity for the orbit, not for the full matrix space minus the pair orbit. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 **Chain strata.** Stratify $Z$ by its compatible alternating-string diagrams at every link. Compatibility means that the $b$-diagram of one link equals the $a$-diagram of the next. These are finitely many locally closed strata. Pair-orbit projections to either ordinary Jordan orbit are smooth homogeneous fibrations: their fibers are quotients of the ordinary centralizer unit group by the pair stabilizer. Both groups are smooth connected open subsets of finite-dimensional endomorphism spaces, so these fibers are irreducible. Iterating these fibrations proves each nonempty chain stratum $Z_\delta$ smooth and irreducible. The dimension at each fiber-product step is the preceding dimension plus the pair-orbit dimension minus the shared Jordan-orbit dimension. The intermediate orbit dimensions cancel in the formula of step 2.1, giving $\dim Z_\delta=\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12\dim C_\sigma-\sum_{i<t}\Delta_i$, where $\sigma$ is the type of its final end map. [F2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 **Dominance and the top stratum.** The chain equations make $\theta^k$ factor through $U_{t-k}$, so $\operatorname{rank}\theta^k\le n_{t-k}$ and $\theta^t=0$. Thus its type $\sigma$ is dominated by $\eta$ by [F3]. For a $b$-diagram $\sigma$, every row must first be filled internally by alternating $a$ letters; this requires exactly $|\sigma|-\ell(\sigma)$ letters, the size of the diagram obtained by deleting its first column. Over the top diagram $\eta$, this equals $n_{t-1}$, leaving no extra letters: every string starts and ends in $b$ and the lower diagram is exactly the first-column deletion of $\eta$. Repeat down the chain. There is exactly one top stratum; it has both maximal-rank maps at every link, lies in $Z^\circ$, and has every $\Delta_i=0$. Finally, expanding $q_j=n_{t-j+1}-n_{t-j}$ gives $\tfrac12\dim C_\eta=\sum_{i<t}n_in_{i+1}-\sum_{i<t}n_i^2$, so its dimension is $D$. [F3, step 1.3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 **Drops of at least four.** By the stratum formula and the nonnegativity of all $\Delta_i$, a final orbit drop of at least four gives $\dim Z_\delta\le\sum n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12(\dim C_\eta-4)=D-2$. Every non-top stratum has dimension at most $D-1$. This latter estimate establishes uniqueness of the dense top stratum but does not assert that every non-top stratum has codimension two: some are smooth divisors inside $Z^\circ$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 1.4, algebra]

6.1 **Drops of two and the nonsmooth-locus bound.** Suppose $\sigma$ is obtained from $\eta$ by moving a box to the next row. Let $\eta'$ and $\sigma'$ denote first-column deletions and let $m=|\eta'|$, $m'=|\sigma'|$. At the last link the available number of $a$ letters is $m$ and its $a$-diagram must be dominated by $\eta'$, since its powers factor through the shorter chain. If the receiving row was nonempty, $m=m'$: internal filling consumes every $a$, all strings begin and end in $b$, and the same next-row degeneration passes to the shorter chain. If a new singleton row is created, $m=m'+1$. After internal filling there is one extra $a$. It can be attached at either end of the shortened last row, at either end of the new singleton $b$ row, or placed in a new singleton $a$ row. No earlier row can receive it: its $a$-diagram would gain a box earlier than the removed last-row box and violate dominance by $\eta'$. In the first four placements one map is maximal rank; the lower diagram is either $\eta'$ or its next-row degeneration. In the fifth placement both maps fail maximal rank, and singleton strings of both types occur, giving $\Delta_i\ge1$. This remains valid when the shortened row is itself a singleton, when there can be more than one singleton $b$. Inducting through the shorter chain shows that either every link has a maximal-rank map and $Z_\delta\subseteq Z^\circ$, or some $\Delta_i\ge1$. In the latter case the dimension formula gives $\dim Z_\delta\le\sum n_in_{i+1}+\tfrac12(\dim C_\eta-2)-1=D-2$. Together with step 5.1, this proves $\dim(Z\setminus Z^\circ)\le D-2$. [step 1.3, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 1.4, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 **Complete intersection and reducedness.** Every irreducible component of the scheme cut out by its $c$ equations has dimension at least $\dim M-c=D$ by [F4]. The top stratum has dimension $D$ and all other strata have smaller dimension by step 5.1, so every component has dimension $D$. Thus the equation ideal has height $c$. Its homogeneous generators form a regular sequence in the polynomial ring: at the homogeneous maximal ideal, every prefix of length $k$ has height at least $k$, since adjoining the remaining $c-k$ equations raises height by at most $c-k$; the opposite inequality is Krull's bound. Complete the generators to a system of parameters and apply the Cohen-Macaulay parameter theorem in [F4]. Homogeneous localization detects a kernel in a multiplication map, so regularity is global. The quotient is Cohen-Macaulay, hence satisfies $S_1$ and $S_2$. Every component meets the smooth open $Z^\circ$ by step 6.1, so it satisfies $R_0$; [F5] implies reducedness. [F4, F5, step 1.2, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 **Irreducibility and normality of the chain.** The unique top stratum is irreducible. Its closure contains every component: otherwise a component of dimension $D$ would have a nonempty open subset outside that closure, contained in a finite union of strata of dimensions at most $D-1$, which is impossible. Thus the reduced chain ring is a domain. Its singular locus is contained in $Z\setminus Z^\circ$, of codimension at least two by step 6.1, so it satisfies $R_1$; it satisfies $S_2$ by step 7.1. Serre's criterion [F5] gives normality. [F5, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 **The invariant quotient.** For one pair $A:U\to W$, $B:W\to U$, invariants under $\mathrm{GL}(U)$ are generated by entries of $AB$: the scalar matrices force equal polynomial degrees in $A,B$, polarization turns a bihomogeneous invariant into a mixed tensor invariant, and [F6] expresses it as permutation contractions. Each contraction is a product of entries of $AB$, with possible cyclic traces also polynomials in those entries. For rational finite-dimensional $\mathrm{GL}(U)$ modules, the central scalar torus splits the space into integer weight spaces. On each weight space apply the semisimple Lie algebra complete-reducibility theorem [F6] to $\mathfrak{sl}(U)$; an invariant complement then respects the center as well. It respects the group because elementary unipotents and diagonal matrices generate $\mathrm{GL}(U)$. Thus rational quotient invariants lift by complete reducibility in bounded polynomial degree, so the same description applies to a stable closed subscheme with its induced relations. Eliminate vertices in order. At the first vertex the invariant generators are $A_1B_1$ and the remaining variables; the chain equation replaces $A_1B_1$ by $B_2A_2$. The quotient is consequently the graph over the remaining variables with the induced rank and nilpotency relations, and eliminating the next vertex applies the same one-pair calculation. Repeating leaves precisely the entries of $\theta$. Thus $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ is generated by those entries, and is the coordinate ring of the closure of $\theta(Z)$. The rank bounds of step 4.1 put the image in the orbit closure of $e$, while the inclusion/restriction construction of step 1.2, applied to every conjugate of $e$, puts its full orbit in the image. Hence that closure is $X$ and $\mathbb C[Z]^H\cong\mathbb C[X]$. [F1, F3, F6, step 1.2, step 4.1, step 8.1, algebra]

10.1 **Normality and boundary of the orbit closure.** An element of $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb C[Z]^H)$ integral over $\mathbb C[Z]^H$ is also integral over the normal domain $\mathbb C[Z]$, hence belongs to it. Being a fraction of invariant elements it is fixed by $H$, so it belongs to $\mathbb C[Z]^H$; no equality between the full invariant fraction field and the fraction field of the invariant ring is needed. Therefore $\mathbb C[X]$ is a normal domain, reduced and irreducible. The finitely many boundary nilpotent orbits have positive even dimension drops by step 1.4, so their union has codimension at least two. The point cases and their empty boundary were proved in step 1.1. This proves all chain and orbit conclusions. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.4, step 8.1, step 9.1, algebra] ∎

Section 6, printed pp. 245-246, supplies only the companion covariant-extension result. items.title: Arakawa-Suzuki Casimir operators on tensor functors
items.statement:
Work over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]],
[[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). Fix $N\ge1$, let
$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with its matrix units $E_{ij}$ and the
trace form $B(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(XY)$, which is symmetric, nondegenerate and
invariant ([[prop-trace-forms-are-symmetric-and-invariant]]), and let
$$z:=\sum_{i=1}^NE_{ii}\in\mathfrak g$$
be the central element (the identity matrix). The dual basis of $(E_{ij})$
under $B$ is $(E_{ji})$, so the invariant Casimir tensor is
$$\Omega=\sum_{i,j=1}^NE_{ij}\otimes E_{ji}\in U(\mathfrak g)\otimes U(\mathfrak g),$$
Its action on a tensor product of two $\mathfrak g$-modules commutes with the diagonal action, as computed in [F2]. Multiplying its two factors gives the central Casimir element of [[def-casimir-operator-relative-to-an-invariant-form]].

Let $M$ be a $\mathfrak g$-module and $V=\mathbb C^N$ the natural module
([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]). On the tensor product
$M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]],
[[thm-associativity-of-balanced-tensor-products]]) label the factors
$0,1,\dots,d$, with factor $0$ equal to $M$. For $0\le a\ne b\le d$ let
$\Omega_{ab}$ denote the operator obtained by applying $\Omega$ in the two
labelled factors, and for distinct $1\le a,b\le d$ let $P_{ab}$ denote the
operator that interchanges the two labelled factors (the flip of
$V\otimes V$ on two $V$-factors). Define, for $1\le j\le d$ and
$1\le i\le d-1$,
$$x_j:=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}P_{kj},\qquad s_i:=P_{i,i+1}.$$
Finally put $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}:=\Omega-\tfrac1Nz\otimes z$ and define the
Arakawa-Suzuki normalized operators
$$y_j:=x_j-\tfrac1Nz_M+\tfrac{N-1}{2},$$
where $z_M$ denotes the endomorphism of $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ given by the
action of $z$ on the factor $M$. This is a central endomorphism, and is a scalar only when $z$ acts scalarly on $M$.

The verification below records the properties of these operators used on this
page: $\Omega$ acts on $V\otimes V$ as the flip; the operators $x_j$ and
$s_i$ are natural in $M$ and commute with the $\mathfrak g$-action; the
recursion $x_{j+1}=s_jx_js_j+s_j$ holds; $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}$ is the Casimir
of $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ relative to the restricted trace form; and the operators
$y_j$ are exactly the source operators of [AS, (2.2.2)]. For $d=0$ the family
$(x_j)$ is empty; for the trivial module $M=\mathbb C$ one has $\Omega_{0j}=0$,
so $x_j=\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$ and $x_1=0$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The data of [F1]-[F5] and the operators of the Definition.

1.1 $\Omega$ is the flip on $V\otimes V$. On the tensor basis, $\Omega(v_a\otimes v_b)=\sum_{i,j}(E_{ij}v_a)\otimes(E_{ji}v_b)=\sum_{i,j}\delta_{ja}v_i\otimes\delta_{ib}v_j=v_b\otimes v_a=P_{01}(v_a\otimes v_b)$ by [F1]. Consequently $\Omega_{ab}=P_{ab}$ whenever the two labelled factors $a,b$ are both natural factors; in particular $\Omega_{j,j+1}=s_j$ on the $V$-factors. [F1, F3, algebra]

1.2 Naturality and commutation with $\mathfrak g$. For a $\mathfrak g$-module map $f\colon M\to M'$, the map $f\otimes1^{\otimes d}$ intertwines $x_j$ and $s_i$: it plainly intertwines the place permutations $P_{ab}$, and it intertwines $\Omega_{0j}$ because the Casimir operator on a tensor product of modules is an intertwiner by [F2]. For the same reason each $x_j$ and $s_i$ commutes with the $\mathfrak g$-action on $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$, the action on the $V$-factors being the natural one. [F2, F3, algebra]

1.3 The $\mathfrak{sl}_N$ Casimir. The trace form restricts to a nondegenerate form on $\mathfrak{sl}_N$: $\mathfrak{sl}_N=\{X\in\mathfrak g:B(X,z)=0\}$ because $B(X,z)=\operatorname{tr}(X)$ and $B(z,z)=N\ne0$. Hence $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}=\Omega-\frac1Nz\otimes z$ is the inverse tensor of $B|_{\mathfrak{sl}_N}$: for $X\in\mathfrak{sl}_N$, contracting the second factor of $\Omega$ with $X$ gives $\sum_{ij}B(X,E_{ji})E_{ij}=X$, while contracting the second factor of $z\otimes z$ with $X$ gives $B(X,z)z=\operatorname{tr}(X)z=0$; so contraction with $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}$ also returns $X$, and by [F2] the dual tensor is unique. Thus $\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}$ is the $\mathfrak{sl}_N$-Casimir for the restricted trace form. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The recursion. Since $s_j=P_{j,j+1}$ and $P_{ab}$ are involutions with $P_{ab}\Omega_{ab}P_{ab}=\Omega_{ab}$ and conjugation by $P_{j,j+1}$ replaces the label $j$ by $j+1$ in every operator supported on labels $\{0,1,\dots,j\}$, one has $s_j\Omega_{0j}s_j=\Omega_{0,j+1}$, $s_jP_{kj}s_j=P_{k,j+1}$ for $k<j$, and $s_js_j=1$. Hence $s_jx_js_j+s_j=\Omega_{0,j+1}+\sum_{k<j}P_{k,j+1}+P_{j,j+1}=x_{j+1}$, using $x_{j+1}=\Omega_{0,j+1}+\sum_{k<j+1}P_{k,j+1}$ and $P_{j,j+1}=s_j$. Thus the operators satisfy the recursion of [F4]. The remaining Hecke relations require the independent commutator check in [[thm-the-casimir-and-place-permutation-operators-satisfy-degenerate-affine-hecke-relations]]. [F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The source dictionary. Let $\Omega$ now denote the $\mathfrak{sl}_N$-Casimir in the formula (2.2.1) of the source [F5], so that on two natural factors $\Omega_{ij}=P_{ij}-1/N$ by steps 1.1 and 1.3, i.e. $P_{ij}=\Omega_{ij}+1/N$, which is exactly [AS, (2.2.1)]. On $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ the library $\mathfrak{gl}_N$-Casimir satisfies $\Omega^{\mathfrak{gl}_N}_{0j}=\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}_{0j}+z_M/N$ (the extra term $\frac1Nz\otimes z$ acts on factor $0$ as $z_M/N$ and on factor $j$ as the identity on $V$), while $\Omega^{\mathfrak{gl}_N}_{kj}=\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}_{kj}+1/N$ for two natural factors; therefore $y_j=x_j-\tfrac1Nz_M+\tfrac{N-1}{2}=\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}(\Omega^{\mathrm{sl}}_{kj}+\tfrac1N)+\tfrac{N-1}{2}$, which is precisely the source formula (2.2.2) in [F5]. [F5, step 1.1, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Special cases. For $d=0$ there are no labels $j\ge1$, so the family $(x_j)$ and $(s_i)$ is empty and the Definition records only the module $M$; the recursion and the dictionary are vacuous. For the trivial module $M=\mathbb C$ the action of $\mathfrak g$ is zero, so $\Omega_{0j}=0$ and $z_M=0$; hence $x_j=\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$, with the empty sum $x_1=0$. [F1, F3, given] ∎

references.title: Tomoyuki Arakawa and Takeshi Suzuki, Lie algebras and degenerate affine Hecke algebras of type A, J. Algebra 209 (1998) 288-304 (complete 16-page arXiv preprint of the origin paper)
references.locator: Sections 1.2 and 2.2, printed pp. 6-7: the sl_n Casimir Omega, the operators (2.2.1) s_ij=Omega_ij+1/n and (2.2.2) y_i=Omega_0i+sum_{1<=j<i}(Omega_ji+1/n)+(n-1)/2, Lemma 2.2.1 and Theorem 2.2.2 on the resulting H_l-action.

references.title: Jonathan Brundan and Alexander Kleshchev, Schur-Weyl duality for higher levels, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 14 (2008) 1-57 (complete 50-page arXiv article)
references.locator: Introduction, printed pp. 1-2: for Omega=sum_{i,j} e_ij tensor e_ji the action of x_1 as Omega tensor 1^{tensor d-1} and of s_i as the place permutation, with the resulting right H_d-action on M tensor V^{tensor d} commuting with gl_n.

items.title: Nilpotent-orbit tensor covariants extend and polarize
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $e$ be a nilpotent endomorphism of a
finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$, let
$G_e=\{g\in\mathrm{GL}(V):geg^{-1}=e\}$ be its centralizer, and let $d\ge0$.

1. Every $G_e$-fixed endomorphism $B\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V^{\otimes d})$
   is the value at $e$ of a $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-equivariant polynomial map
   $\Phi\colon\operatorname{End}(V)\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$
   (polynomial in the matrix entries of the input, with
   $\Phi(gXg^{-1})=(g^{\otimes d})\Phi(X)(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}$).
2. Every such equivariant polynomial map is a finite sum
   $\Phi(X)=\sum_hc_h\,\sigma_h(X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d})$ with
   $h_i\ge0$, where $\sigma_h$ is a place permutation of the $d$ tensor
   factors and $c_h$ is an invariant scalar polynomial in $X$ (a polynomial
   in the traces $\operatorname{tr}(X^k)$).

The extension in (1) is proved by Hartogs lifting on the normal codimension-$\ge2$
orbit closure; the structure in (2) is proved by polarization and the
Schur-Weyl description of tensor invariants, not by importing a
first-fundamental-theorem for the full matrix algebra.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The data of [F1]-[F4]: the nilpotent $e$, the normal orbit closure $X$ with dense orbit $O$, the connected centralizer $G_e$, the degree $d$, and a $G_e$-fixed $B\in\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$.

1.1 **The zero-dimensional case.** If $V=0$, its orbit closure is a point and its boundary is empty by [F1]. For $d=0$, $V^{\otimes d}=\mathbb C$ and every fixed operator is a scalar, extended by the constant polynomial map; the empty permutation and empty tensor product give the asserted normal form. For $d>0$, $V^{\otimes d}=0$ and its endomorphism space has only the zero operator, extended by the zero map; the normal form is the empty sum. Thus both assertions hold without a largest Jordan block. Henceforth $V\ne0$, so its largest block length $l$ exists. [F1, construct, algebra]

1.2 Hartogs lifting. Let $A=\mathbb C[X]$ and let $f\in\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ be regular on $O$, hence regular off a closed subset of $X\setminus O$; since $\partial X$ has codimension $\ge2$ in $X$ by the normality lemma [F1], $f$ is regular in codimension $1$ and therefore extends to $A$ by [F2]. Applying this coordinatewise to maps into a finite-dimensional vector space shows that every regular map $O\to W$ into a finite-dimensional vector space extends uniquely to a regular map $X\to W$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 The equivariant map on $O$. Fix $B\in\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})^{G_e}$ and define, for $g\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, $F(g\,e\,g^{-1}):=(g^{\otimes d})\,B\,(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}\in\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$. This is well defined: if $g_1e g_1^{-1}=g_2eg_2^{-1}$, then $g_2^{-1}g_1\in G_e$, so $(g_2^{-1}g_1)^{\otimes d}B(g_2^{-1}g_1)^{-\otimes d}=B$ by $G_e$-invariance, which rearranges to $(g_1^{\otimes d})B(g_1^{-1})^{\otimes d}=(g_2^{\otimes d})B(g_2^{-1})^{\otimes d}$. The map $F$ is $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-equivariant by construction: $F(hXh^{-1})=(h^{\otimes d})F(X)(h^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ for $X\in O$. [F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Regularity of $F$ on $O$. The ranks of $X^0,X^1,\dots,X^{l-1}$ are constant on $O$. Cover $O$ by open charts where fixed minors used to select bases of the kernels and images, their quotient complements and Jordan top vectors are nonzero. Gaussian elimination on such a chart gives a Jordan basis for $X$ with entries regular in $X$. Let $g(X)$ carry a fixed Jordan basis for $e$ to this chosen Jordan basis for $X$, with the same ordered string lengths. Then $g(X)e g(X)^{-1}=X$. Restricting to the open chart where the Jordan-basis determinant is nonzero makes both $g(X)$ and $g(X)^{-1}$ regular, since their entries have only the fixed nonvanishing minors and determinant as denominators. Thus $X\mapsto(g(X)^{\otimes d})B(g(X)^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ is the map of step 1.3 and is regular on each chart. These charts cover $O$; on overlaps $g_2(X)^{-1}g_1(X)\in G_e$, so the expressions agree by $G_e$-invariance of $B$. Hence $F$ is regular on $O$. [F1, step 1.3, algebra, construct]

3.1 Extension to $X$. By steps 1.2 and 2.1 the map $F\colon O\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ is a regular equivariant map on the dense orbit; by step 1.2 it extends uniquely to a regular map $F\colon X\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$. Since $\mathbb C[X]=\mathbb C[\operatorname{End}(V)]/I(X)$ and $X$ is an affine closed subset of the affine space $\operatorname{End}(V)$, the coordinate functions of $F$ are restrictions of polynomial functions on $\operatorname{End}(V)$; fixing representatives gives a polynomial map $\Phi\colon\operatorname{End}(V)\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ extending $F$. [F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Equivariance of $\Phi$. For fixed $g\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$, both sides of $\Phi(gXg^{-1})=(g^{\otimes d})\Phi(X)(g^{-1})^{\otimes d}$ are polynomial maps in $X$; they agree on the dense orbit $O$ by step 1.3 and hence on all of $X$. Consequently the class of $\Phi$ in the finite-dimensional space of polynomial maps $\operatorname{End}(V)\to\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ of degree at most $K$ (for $K$ at least the degree of $\Phi$), modulo the $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-stable subspace of maps vanishing on $X$, is invariant for the conjugation action. By the invariant-lifting property of complete reducibility [F3], this class has an invariant representative $\Phi'$ of degree at most $K$; then $\Phi'$ is a $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-equivariant polynomial map on $\operatorname{End}(V)$ agreeing with $F$ on $X$, and $\Phi'(e)=F(e)=B$ since $e\in O$, which is assertion (1). [F3, step 1.3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Polarization. Write $\Phi=\sum_k\Phi_k$ for its homogeneous components of degree $k$; each $\Phi_k$ is equivariant. Fix $k$ and assume for the structure argument that $\Phi$ is homogeneous of degree $k$. Polarize the $k$ matrix variables $X_1,\dots,X_k$ of $\Phi$ and pair the output in $\operatorname{End}(V^{\otimes d})$ with $d$ independent matrices $Y_1,\dots,Y_d$ using the nondegenerate trace pairing on each tensor factor; this produces a multilinear $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-invariant $P(X_1,\dots,X_k;Y_1,\dots,Y_d)\in\mathbb C$ in $(k+d)$ matrix arguments. [F4, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Tensor invariants are permutation contractions. By the Schur-Weyl description [F3], every multilinear invariant of the matrix arguments is a linear combination of contractions: each argument contributes one upper and one lower index, an invariant pairs each upper index with a lower index of another argument, and the invariant is a product over the cycles of the resulting permutation of traces of the corresponding cyclically ordered product of matrices. [F3, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Covariant normal form. Depolarize in the $k$ identical variables $X_i=X$ and read each contraction cycle. A cycle that uses only $X$-arguments contributes a scalar invariant polynomial in $X$; a cycle that uses some $Y$-arguments alternates blocks of $X$'s and single $Y$'s, so its trace is precisely the trace pairing of $Y_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Y_d$ with a place permutation of $X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d}$. By nondegeneracy of the trace pairing, the operator identity $\Phi(X)=\sum_hc_h(X)\,\sigma_h(X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d})$ follows, with $h_i\ge0$, $\sigma_h$ a place permutation and $c_h$ a scalar invariant polynomial (a polynomial in the traces $\operatorname{tr}(X^m)$); summing over the homogeneous components gives assertion (2). [F4, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 Evaluation at $e$. Since $e^l=0$ for the largest Jordan block length $l$ of $e$, evaluating the normal form at $X=e$ kills every term with some $h_i\ge l$; the surviving terms are place permutations applied to a tensor product of nonnegative powers $e^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e^{h_d}$ multiplied by the scalar invariants $c_h(e)$, which are complex constants; since $\operatorname{tr}(e^m)=0$ for every positive $m$, the scalar invariant polynomials satisfy $c_h(e)=c_h(0)$. This gives the concrete description of the $G_e$-fixed endomorphisms used by the double centralizer theorem. [step 7.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: The type-A nilpotent pyramid, good grading and Whittaker character
items.statement: Let $\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$ be a partition of $N$ with transpose $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l\ge0$ and let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$. Number the boxes of the diagram of $\lambda$ by $1,\dots,N$ down columns from the left, write $\mathrm{row}(i),\mathrm{col}(i)$ for the row and column of the $i$-th box, let $L(i)$ and $R(i)$ be the numbers of its immediate left and right neighbours (or $\emptyset$ if absent), and define the nilpotent $e=\sum_{i:L(i)\ne\emptyset}e_{L(i),i}\in\mathfrak g$, $v_i\mapsto v_{L(i)}$. Declare $\deg e_{i,j}=\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)$ and let $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb Z}\mathfrak g_r$, $\mathfrak p=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}\mathfrak g_r$, $\mathfrak h=\mathfrak g_0$, $\mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r<0}\mathfrak g_r$. Then $e\in\mathfrak g_1$ has Jordan type $\lambda$ (largest Jordan block $l$), $\mathfrak p$ is a parabolic subalgebra with Levi factor $\mathfrak h\cong\mathfrak{gl}_{q_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_{q_l}$ and nilradical $\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$, $\mathfrak m$ is the nilradical of the opposite parabolic, $\mathfrak g^{e}$ is the graded subalgebra $\bigoplus_{r\ge0}(\mathfrak g_r\cap\mathfrak g^e)$ generated by the elements $e_{i,j;r}=\sum_{\substack{\mathrm{row}(h)=i,\mathrm{row}(k)=j\\ \mathrm{col}(k)-\mathrm{col}(h)=r}}e_{h,k}$ for $s_{i,j}\le r<p_j$ (where $s_{i,j}=p_j-p_i$ for $i\le j$ and $s_{i,j}=0$ for $i\ge j$), Put $I_{box}=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, $J=\{(a,b)\in I_{box}^2:\mathrm{col}(a)\le\mathrm{col}(b),\ R(b)=\emptyset\}$ and $K=\{(i,j,r):1\le i,j\le n,\ s_{i,j}\le r<p_j\}$. The map $(a,b)\mapsto(\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b),\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a))$ is a bijection $J\to K$. Its inverse takes $b$ to the rightmost box of row $j$ and $a$ to the box in row $i$ at column $p_j-r$. The finite sum $\xi_{a,b}=\sum_{t=0}^{\mathrm{col}(a)-1}e_{L^t(a),L^t(b)}$ equals $e_{\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b);\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)}$; these elements for $(a,b)\in J$ form the same basis of $\mathfrak g^e$ as the elements indexed by $K$. Finally set $\chi(x)=(x,e)=\mathrm{tr}(xe)$ for $x\in\mathfrak m$; then $\chi$ is a Lie algebra character, i.e. $\chi([\mathfrak m,\mathfrak m])=0$. This grading is the type-A pyramid good grading, not the Dynkin grading of an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple; it is the one used for the finite W-algebra of the higher-level Schur-Weyl duality.
items.strategy: Assume AC and work over C. Check [E_ab,E_cd]=delta_bc E_ad−delta_ad E_cb and e v_i=v_L(i). Each row is one Jordan string. For Hom between strings of lengths p_a,p_b, the sl2 decomposition has top grading2(p_b−k)≥0 and bottom−2(p_a−k)≤0, 1≤k≤min(p_a,p_b), under the doubled grading. This proves injectivity/surjectivity of ad e in the negative/nonnegative degrees and the stated centralizer basis, rather than importing the Dynkin grading. The column blocks give the parabolic and opposite radical. Since brackets of negative degrees have degree≤−2 while e has degree1, trace([m,m]e)=0. The undoubled source grading has e degree1; its doubled version has no odd degrees and e degree2. For fixed row labels i,j, the right endpoint b has column p_j. Requiring a at column p_j−r to exist in row i is exactly max(0,p_j−p_i)≤r<p_j, the declared K range. This proves the bijection with J. Successive left shifts terminate after col(a) terms, give every row-pair matrix unit of the same displacement, and commute with e by cancellation of adjacent summands and the right-end boundary. The string calculation gives min(p_i,p_j) independent maps per row pair, so these finite sums are the full centralizer basis. The loop consumers use (i,j,r)∈K and T^(r+1), without confusing box and row indices.

items.title: The Casimir and place-permutation operators satisfy the degenerate affine Hecke relations
items.statement:
Let $N\ge1$, let $M$ be a $\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$-module, let
$V=\mathbb C^N$ be the natural module, and on $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$ use the
operators $x_j=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$ and $s_i=P_{i,i+1}$ of
[[def-arakawa-suzuki-casimir-operators-on-tensor-functors]]. Then:

1. The operators $x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ commute with the
   $\mathfrak g$-action and are natural in $M$, and satisfy all the defining
   relations of the degenerate affine Hecke algebra
   [[def-degenerate-affine-hecke-algebra]]: the Coxeter relations for the
   $s_i$; $s_ix_j=x_js_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$; $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i+1$ and
   $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i+1$; and the polynomial commutation $[x_i,x_j]=0$.
2. Consequently they define, via the generator-fixing anti-involution of the
   Hecke algebra, a natural right $H_d$-action on $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$
   commuting with the left $\mathfrak g$-action.

The commutation of the $x_i$ is an independent check: it does not follow from
the braid relations of the $s_i$ alone.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The operators $x_j=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{k<j}P_{kj}$ and $s_i=P_{i,i+1}$ on $M\otimes V^{\otimes d}$, and the identities of [F1]-[F5].

1.1 The infinitesimal braid identities. For distinct labels $a,b,c$ one has $[\Omega_{ab},\Omega_{ac}+\Omega_{bc}]=0$: expanding $\Omega=\sum E_{uv}\otimes E_{vu}$ and using [F3], the double commutator sum splits into terms $[E_{uv},E_{xy}]\otimes E_{vu}\otimes E_{yx}$ and $E_{uv}\otimes[E_{vu},E_{xy}]\otimes E_{yx}$, and the two resulting sums cancel term by term after relabelling; equivalently, this is the identity $[\Omega_{12},\Omega_{13}+\Omega_{23}]=0$ in $U(\mathfrak g)^{\otimes3}$, which is the derivative of the invariance of $\Omega$ under the diagonal adjoint action. Consequently $[\Omega_{ab},\Omega_{ac}]=-[\Omega_{ab},\Omega_{bc}]=[\Omega_{ac},\Omega_{bc}]$. In particular, for three natural factors this is the identity $[P_{ab},P_{ac}]+[P_{ab},P_{bc}]=0$ for the flips. [F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 The Coxeter relations for $s_i$. $s_i=P_{i,i+1}$ is an involution; $s_is_j=s_js_i$ for $|i-j|>1$ because the pairs of interchanged labels are disjoint; and $s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1}$ because both sides are the permutation operator inducing the same permutation of the three labelled factors. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Cross relations. Conjugation by $s_i=P_{i,i+1}$ interchanges the labels $i$ and $i+1$ in any operator supported on those factors, so $s_i\Omega_{0,i+1}=\Omega_{0i}s_i$ and $s_iP_{k,i+1}=P_{ki}s_i$ for $k<i$. Therefore $s_ix_{i+1}=s_i\Omega_{0,i+1}+\sum_{k<i}s_iP_{k,i+1}+s_iP_{i,i+1}=\Omega_{0i}s_i+\sum_{k<i}P_{ki}s_i+1=x_is_i+1$, and symmetrically $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i+1$. For $j<i$, all labels in $x_j$ are disjoint from $\{i,i+1\}$, so $s_i$ commutes with every summand. For $j>i+1$, $\Omega_{0j}$ and the terms $P_{kj}$ with $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$ commute with $s_i$, while conjugation by $s_i$ interchanges $P_{ij}$ and $P_{i+1,j}$. Their sum is invariant, so again $s_ix_j=x_js_i$; the two overlapping summands need not commute individually. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Polynomial commutation. Fix $i<j$. Since $x_i=\Omega_{0i}+\sum_{k<i}P_{ki}$ and $x_j=\Omega_{0j}+\sum_{l<j}P_{lj}$, the commutator is $[\Omega_{0i},\Omega_{0j}]+\sum_{l<j}[\Omega_{0i},P_{lj}]+\sum_{k<i}[P_{ki},\Omega_{0j}]+\sum_{k<i}\sum_{l<j}[P_{ki},P_{lj}]$. The second sum reduces to the single term $[\Omega_{0i},P_{ij}]$ (all other $P_{lj}$ are disjoint from the labels $0,i$), and the third sum vanishes (all pairs $\{k,i\}$, $\{0,j\}$ are disjoint since $k<i<j$). In the fourth sum only the terms with $k=l$ or $l=i$ can fail to vanish, so it equals $\sum_{k<i}([P_{ki},P_{kj}]+[P_{ki},P_{ij}])$. Hence $[x_i,x_j]=([\Omega_{0i},\Omega_{0j}]+[\Omega_{0i},P_{ij}])+\sum_{k<i}([P_{ki},P_{kj}]+[P_{ki},P_{ij}])$. The first bracket vanishes by step 1.1 with $a=0$, $b=i$, $c=j$ together with $\Omega_{ij}=P_{ij}$; each summand of the second bracket vanishes by step 1.1 for the three distinct labels $k,i,j$. Therefore $[x_i,x_j]=0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Naturality, commutation with $\mathfrak g$, and the right action. The place permutations are natural in $M$ and commute with $\mathfrak g$; the Casimir operators are intertwiners by [F5]; hence every $x_j$ and $s_i$ is natural and $\mathfrak g$-linear. The relations established in steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 2.2 are exactly the defining relations of $H_d$ [F4], so the assignment $x_j\mapsto x_j$, $s_i\mapsto s_i$ defines a left $H_d$-action. The generator-fixing anti-automorphism $\omega$ of $H_d$ (which preserves each defining relation because the reversed cross relation $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i+1$ is also a defining relation) converts it into a right action by $e\cdot u:=\rho(\omega(u))e$; the anti-automorphism property gives $(e\cdot u)\cdot v=\rho(\omega(v))\rho(\omega(u))e=\rho(\omega(uv))e=e\cdot(uv)$. This proves both assertions. [F4, F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

references.locator: Lemma 2.2.1, printed p. 7, and its proof: [y_i,y_j]=0 from [Omega_ij+Omega_jk,Omega_ik]=0 and [Omega_ij,Omega_km]=0 for distinct labels, and the cross relation (2.2.4) from s_iOmega_0j=Omega_0s_i(j)s_i.

items.title: The type-A finite W-algebra and the Whittaker category
items.statement:
Keep the type-A pyramid data
$(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak p,\mathfrak h,\mathfrak m,e,\chi)$ of
[[def-a-type-a-nilpotent-pyramid-good-grading-and-whittaker-character]], with
$\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$, transpose
$q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, and $\chi(x)=\operatorname{tr}(xe)$ on $\mathfrak m$.
Let $\eta\colon U(\mathfrak p)\to U(\mathfrak p)$ be the algebra automorphism
with
$$\eta(e_{i,j})=e_{i,j}+\delta_{i,j}\bigl(n-q_{\mathrm{col}(j)}-q_{\mathrm{col}(j)+1}-\cdots-q_l\bigr)$$
for all matrix units $e_{i,j}\in\mathfrak p$. Let $I_\chi$ be the kernel of the
algebra homomorphism $\chi\colon U(\mathfrak m)\to\mathbb C$ extending the Lie
character $\chi$, that is, the two-sided ideal generated by $x-\chi(x)$,
$x\in\mathfrak m$ ([[def-universal-enveloping-algebra]],
[[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]], [[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]),
and let $U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ be the left ideal it generates in
$U(\mathfrak g)$.

The **type-A finite W-algebra** is
$$W(\lambda)=\{u\in U(\mathfrak p):[x,\eta(u)]\in U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi\ \text{for all }x\in\mathfrak m\}.$$
It is a subalgebra of $U(\mathfrak p)$, and
$Q_\chi=U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ is a
$(U(\mathfrak g),W(\lambda))$-bimodule with right action
$\bar v\cdot u=\overline{v\,\eta(u)}$. This is a module quotient by a left ideal; no quotient-ring multiplication is imposed.

The **Whittaker category** $\mathcal C(\lambda)$ is the category of
$\mathfrak g$-modules on which $x-\chi(x)$ acts locally nilpotently for every
$x\in\mathfrak m$ ([[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]). For
$M\in\mathcal C(\lambda)$ the **Whittaker vectors**
$$\mathrm{Wh}(M)=\{v\in M:xv=\chi(x)v\ \text{for all }x\in\mathfrak m\}$$
form a $W(\lambda)$-module with $u\cdot v=\eta(u)v$, and
$\mathrm{Wh}(M)=0$ implies $M=0$.

The verification below establishes the algebra and module structures just
stated. The associated graded of the loop filtration on $U(\mathfrak p)$ makes
$W(\lambda)$ a filtered deformation of $U(\mathfrak g^e)$; that statement is
proved later on this page
([[thm-the-loop-filtration-on-the-type-a-finite-w-algebra-has-associated-graded-u-of-g-e]]),
and the filtration used is the loop (good) filtration, not the Kazhdan
filtration.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The pyramid data, the automorphism $\eta$, the ideal $I_\chi$ and the left ideal $U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$.

1.1 Write $c_j=n-q_{\operatorname{col}(j)}-\cdots-q_l$. The scalar functional $\kappa(e_{ij})=\delta_{ij}c_j$ kills $[\mathfrak p,\mathfrak p]$: a bracket can have a diagonal component only from $e_{ij},e_{ji}\in\mathfrak p$, forcing equal columns and equal $c_i,c_j$. Thus $x\mapsto x+\kappa(x)1$ preserves brackets and extends to $\eta$ by the enveloping universal property; the negative scalar shift is its inverse. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Put $J=U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$. For $v\in W$ and $x\in\mathfrak m$, $(x-\chi(x))\eta(v)=\eta(v)(x-\chi(x))+[x,\eta(v)]\in J$. Since these shifted generators generate $J$ as a left ideal, $J\eta(v)\subseteq J$. Hence for $u,v\in W$, $[x,\eta(uv)]=[x,\eta(u)]\eta(v)+\eta(u)[x,\eta(v)]\in J$, using this normalizer property for the first term and the left-ideal property for the second. Additivity, scalar closure and $[x,1]=0$ give a unital subalgebra. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Left multiplication makes $Q_\chi=U(\mathfrak g)/J$ a left module. Step 2.1 proves that $\bar a\cdot u=\overline{a\eta(u)}$ is well defined for $u\in W$. Since $\eta(uv)=\eta(u)\eta(v)$, $(\bar a\cdot u)\cdot v=\bar a\cdot(uv)$, and left multiplication commutes with this right action. Thus $Q_\chi$ is the stated bimodule, with right-action homomorphism into $\operatorname{End}_{U(\mathfrak g)}(Q_\chi)^{\mathrm{op}}$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 $\mathrm{Wh}(M)$ is a $W(\lambda)$-module. Let $M\in\mathcal C(\lambda)$ and $v\in\mathrm{Wh}(M)$. First, $uv=\chi(u)v$ for every $u\in U(\mathfrak m)$: this holds for $u\in\mathfrak m$ by definition and extends to products by induction, since if $yv=\chi(y)v$ then $(xy)v=x(yv)=\chi(y)xv=\chi(x)\chi(y)v$. Hence $I_\chi v=0$, because $I_\chi=\ker(\chi\colon U(\mathfrak m)\to\mathbb C)$ and every element of $I_\chi$ acts on $v$ by its $\chi$-value, which is zero. Consequently $U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi\cdot v=0$, since a general element of $U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ is a sum of products $a\,i$ with $a\in U(\mathfrak g)$, $i\in I_\chi$, and $(ai)v=a(iv)=0$. Now take $u\in W(\lambda)$, $x\in\mathfrak m$. Then $x(\eta(u)v)=\eta(u)xv+[x,\eta(u)]v=\chi(x)\eta(u)v+0$, because $[x,\eta(u)]\in U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ by the definition of $W(\lambda)$. Hence $\eta(u)v\in\mathrm{Wh}(M)$, and the map $(u,v)\mapsto\eta(u)v$ is bilinear and associative by the algebra structure of $U(\mathfrak p)$ and step 1.1. Here the character $\chi$ and the parabolic data are those of [F1]. This verifies the module structure; the vanishing statement $\mathrm{Wh}(M)=0\Rightarrow M=0$ is the cohomological detection theorem proved in [[lem-gan-ginzburg-skryabin-inputs-hold-for-the-type-a-pyramid-good-grading]] and [[thm-skryabins-equivalence-for-the-type-a-whittaker-pair]], and is recorded here as part of the categorical interface. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
