items.title: The regular coset-dominant Harish–Chandra tensor comparison

references.title: Bernstein and Gelfand, Tensor products of finite and infinite dimensional representations of semisimple Lie algebras
references.locator: Sections 5.1–5.12; adoption from the authenticated owner-category-o-batch17-hc-comparison-proof research note, with the projective-presentation argument expanded locally.

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_N(\mathbb C)$,
with upper-triangular Borel, and represent $a=\lambda+\rho$ by coordinates
of sum zero. For every $i<j$ with $a_i-a_j\in\mathbb Z$, require
$a_i-a_j\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$. Thus $a$ is regular and strictly decreasing
inside each coordinate coset modulo $\mathbb Z$; there is no ordering of
complex numbers from different cosets. Write $P$ for the weight lattice,
$U_\chi=U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi_\lambda$, and
$\mathcal O_{\lambda+P}$ for objects of genuine $\mathcal O$ whose weights
belong to $\lambda+P$.

Let $\mathcal H_\chi$ consist of finitely generated $U$-bimodules $B$ with
$B\ker\chi_\lambda=0$ and locally finite adjoint $\mathfrak g$-action.
For finite-dimensional $E$ let $\Phi_E=E\otimes U_\chi$, with diagonal
left action and ordinary right action. Then
$$T_\lambda(B)=B\otimes_U\Delta(\lambda)$$
is an exact equivalence $\mathcal H_\chi\simeq\mathcal O_{\lambda+P}$.
Every object on either side has a finite presentation by the respective
projective generators $\Phi_E$ and $E\otimes\Delta(\lambda)$. The induced
map is the natural, composition-preserving identification
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal H_\chi}(\Phi_E,\Phi_F)\ \cong\ (E^*\otimes F\otimes U_\chi)^{\mathfrak g}\ \cong\ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E\otimes\Delta(\lambda),F\otimes\Delta(\lambda)).$$
The comparison commutes naturally with finite-dimensional tensoring.

For $\mathfrak{gl}_N$ the corresponding statement uses
$\mathcal O_{\lambda+\mathbb Z^N}$ and finite-dimensional modules with
integral coordinate weights; $\mathcal H_\chi$ additionally requires its
adjoint Cartan weights to be integral and its adjoint scalar centre to act
semisimply. No assertion here supplies standard-label transport, a
parabolic restriction, or this equivalence for a nonprojective source
Verma or a singular source weight.
items.strategy: Direct local proof: projectivity at regular coset-dominant lambda, norm and linkage control of tensor flags, finite tensor projective presentations on both sides, Duflo action identification of generator Hom spaces, then cokernel/kernel presentation comparison and the integral-coordinate gl_N centre extension.

items.title: Vust's graded double centralizer for the type-A nilpotent centralizer
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector
space, let $e\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ be nilpotent with largest
Jordan string length $l\ge1$, let $d\ge0$, and put $E=V^{\otimes d}$. Let
$$B=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]/(x_1^l,\dots,x_d^l)\rtimes\mathbb C[S_d]$$
act on $E$ by the individual operators $x_i=e$ (in the $i$-th tensor factor)
and the place permutations, and let
$\varphi\colon U(\mathfrak g^e)\to\operatorname{End}(E)$ be the algebra map
induced by the diagonal action of $\mathfrak g^e=\{X:[X,e]=0\}$ and
$\psi\colon B\to\operatorname{End}(E)^{\mathrm{op}}$ the map encoding the
right action. Then
$$\varphi(U(\mathfrak g^e))=\operatorname{End}_B(E),\qquad \operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g^e}(E)^{\mathrm{op}}=\psi(B),$$
for every nilpotent Jordan type and every $d$. If $e$ has at least $d$ Jordan
strings of the maximum length $l$, then $\psi$ is injective. For $d=0$ the
identities are scalar identities and injectivity is automatic.

The full converse uses the proved normality and covariant-extension suppliers
of this page; it is not a stable-only claim and it does not assume the double
commutant identity.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The algebra $A=\mathfrak g^e$, the truncated algebra $B$, and the maps $\varphi,\psi$ of the Statement.

1.1 The first centralizer. An operator $T\in\operatorname{End}(E)$ commutes with the action of $B$ if and only if it commutes with the individual $e$-operators and with the place permutations: the first condition says $T\in A^{\otimes d}$ by [F2], and then the second says $T\in(A^{\otimes d})^{S_d}$, which is spanned by the elements $a^{\otimes d}$, $a\in A$. The image of $U(\mathfrak g^e)$ under the diagonal representation is contained in $\operatorname{End}_B(E)$: the diagonal action of $A$ commutes with the individual $e$'s and with places. Conversely, for $a\in A$ the element $a^{\otimes d}$ equals the product of its individual-position operators; For the commuting individual operators $a_i$, put $Q(t)=\prod_i(1+a_it)=\sum_r q_rt^r$ and $p_k=\sum_i a_i^k$. Formal differentiation and the geometric series for each factor give $Q'(t)=Q(t)\sum_{k\ge1}(-1)^{k-1}p_kt^{k-1}$, so $q_0=1$ and $q_r=r^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^r(-1)^{k-1}p_kq_{r-k}$. Each $p_k=\Delta_d(a^k)$ belongs to the enveloping image because $A$ is an associative algebra; here $a^k$ is the matrix power, regarded as an element of the Lie algebra $A$. The recurrence therefore puts $q_d=\prod_i a_i=a^{\otimes d}$ in that image. Hence $a^{\otimes d}\in\varphi(U(\mathfrak g^e))$ and $\varphi(U(\mathfrak g^e))=\operatorname{End}_B(E)$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The second centralizer. An operator $T$ commutes with the diagonal $A$-action if and only if it is $G_e$-fixed, as follows. If $T$ is $G_e$-fixed, commuting with $(1+ta)^{\otimes d}$ for all but finitely many $t$ and comparing its linear coefficient gives $[T,\Delta_d(a)]=0$. Conversely, if $T$ commutes with every $\Delta_d(a)$, it commutes with $\Delta_d(a^k)$ for all $k$. Newton identities express $a^{\otimes d}$ in these power sums, so $T$ commutes with $a^{\otimes d}$, in particular for every unit $a\in G_e$. By [F3] every $G_e$-fixed operator is $\Phi(e)$ for an equivariant polynomial covariant $\Phi(X)=\sum_hc_h(X)\sigma_h(X^{h_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes X^{h_d})$; evaluating at $X=e$ replaces each $X^{h_i}$ by $e^{h_i}$, which is a polynomial in the individual $e$-operators of degree less than $l$, so $\Phi(e)\in\psi(B)$ (the truncated algebra $B$ contains exactly the polynomials $e^0,\dots,e^{l-1}$ in each factor and the places). Conversely every element of $\psi(B)$ commutes with the diagonal $A$-action: for $a\in A$ put $\Delta_d(a)=\sum_{k=1}^d a^{(k)}$; each individual $e^{(j)}$ satisfies $[\Delta_d(a),e^{(j)}]=[a,e]^{(j)}=0$, and each place permutation $P_\sigma$ satisfies $P_\sigma\Delta_d(a)P_\sigma^{-1}=\Delta_d(a)$. These operators generate $\psi(B)$, so their products and linear combinations also commute with every $\Delta_d(a)$. Therefore $\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak g^e}(E)^{\mathrm{op}}=\psi(B)$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Stable injectivity. Suppose $e$ has at least $d$ Jordan strings of the maximum length $l$, with top vectors $w_1,\dots,w_d$ on distinct strings. The vectors $w_1^{r_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes w_d^{r_d}$ with $0\le r_i<l$ (where $w^r=e^rw$ is the $r$-th vector of the string) are $l^d$ distinct members of the Jordan tensor basis of $E$; applying the $d!$ place permutations gives $l^d d!$ distinct basis vectors, since the string label of each tensor factor is recovered from the vector and the place permutation is recovered from the ordering of the labels. These vectors span a right $B$-submodule isomorphic to the regular module $B$ (the basis vectors $e^{r_1}w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes e^{r_d}w_d\sigma$, $\sigma\in S_d$, multiply exactly as the standard basis of the truncated polynomial/permutation algebra), so the right action $\psi$ is injective. For $d=0$, $E=\mathbb C$, $B=\mathbb C$ and both identities and injectivity reduce to scalar identities. [F1, F4, algebra, construct] ∎

references.title: Jonathan Brundan and Alexander Kleshchev, Schur-Weyl duality for higher levels, Selecta Math. (N.S.) 14 (2008) 1-57 (complete 50-page arXiv article)
references.locator: Sections 2.1-2.3 and Theorem 2.4, printed pp. 6-9: the graded Schur algebra C[M_e]^*_d and the double centralizer for the pair (U(g^e), C_l[x_1,...,x_d] rtimes C[S_d]) on V^{tensor d}, for every nilpotent Jordan type and every d, with stable injectivity.

references.title: T. Vust, Sur la contraction des espaces de tenseurs, C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 289 (1979) A141-A143
references.locator: The graded double centralizer theorem for the pair of the nilpotent centralizer and the truncated polynomial/permutation algebra, quoted in the source above as Theorem 2.4. The full converse is reconstructed locally in owner-category-o-batch17-vust-local-proof.md, Sections 1, 4 and 5.

items.title: The shifted Yangian and the pyramid generators of the type-A finite W-algebra
items.statement:
Work over $\mathbb C$ and fix $n\ge1$ together with a shift matrix
$\sigma=(s_{i,j})_{1\le i,j\le n}$ of nonnegative integers satisfying
$s_{i,j}+s_{j,k}=s_{i,k}$ whenever $i\le j\le k$ or $i\ge j\ge k$, and
$s_{i,i}=0$. The **shifted Yangian** $Y_n(\sigma)$ is the associative unital
$\mathbb C$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) generated by the
shifted Drinfeld generators $D_i^{(r)}$ ($1\le i\le n$, $r\ge1$),
$E_i^{(r)}$ ($1\le i<n$, $r>s_{i,i+1}$), and
$F_i^{(r)}$ ($1\le i<n$, $r>s_{i+1,i}$). For $i<j$, the higher-root
coefficients $E_{i,j}^{(r)}$ have range $r>s_{i,j}$ and
$F_{j,i}^{(r)}$ have range $r>s_{j,i}$; they are defined recursively by
adjacent-root commutators, not declared as a duplicate independent family.
Put $D_i^{(0)}=1$, $D_i(u)=\sum_{r\ge0}D_i^{(r)}u^{-r}$ and $\widetilde D_i(u)=-D_i(u)^{-1}$. The defining relations are the following, for every index for which all displayed generators exist (in particular the $E$ and $F$ indices exceed their respective shifts):

$$[D_i^{(r)},D_j^{(s)}]=0,\qquad [E_i^{(r)},F_j^{(s)}]=\delta_{ij}\sum_{t=0}^{r+s-1}\widetilde D_i^{(t)}D_{i+1}^{(r+s-1-t)}.$$

$$[D_i^{(r)},E_j^{(s)}]=(\delta_{ij}-\delta_{i,j+1})\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}D_i^{(t)}E_j^{(r+s-1-t)}.$$

$$[D_i^{(r)},F_j^{(s)}]=(\delta_{i,j+1}-\delta_{ij})\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}F_j^{(r+s-1-t)}D_i^{(t)}.$$

$$[E_i^{(r)},E_i^{(s+1)}]-[E_i^{(r+1)},E_i^{(s)}]=E_i^{(r)}E_i^{(s)}+E_i^{(s)}E_i^{(r)}.$$

$$[F_i^{(r+1)},F_i^{(s)}]-[F_i^{(r)},F_i^{(s+1)}]=F_i^{(r)}F_i^{(s)}+F_i^{(s)}F_i^{(r)}.$$

$$[E_i^{(r)},E_{i+1}^{(s+1)}]-[E_i^{(r+1)},E_{i+1}^{(s)}]=-E_i^{(r)}E_{i+1}^{(s)}.$$

$$[F_i^{(r+1)},F_{i+1}^{(s)}]-[F_i^{(r)},F_{i+1}^{(s+1)}]=-F_{i+1}^{(s)}F_i^{(r)}.$$

For $|i-j|>1$, $[E_i^{(r)},E_j^{(s)}]=[F_i^{(r)},F_j^{(s)}]=0$. For $|i-j|=1$ impose

$$[E_i^{(r)},[E_i^{(s)},E_j^{(t)}]]+[E_i^{(s)},[E_i^{(r)},E_j^{(t)}]]=0,$$

$$[F_i^{(r)},[F_i^{(s)},F_j^{(t)}]]+[F_i^{(s)},[F_i^{(r)},F_j^{(t)}]]=0.$$

The higher roots are specified without new independent generators by $E_{i,i+1}^{(r)}=E_i^{(r)}$, $F_{i+1,i}^{(r)}=F_i^{(r)}$, and, for $j>i+1$,

$$E_{i,j}^{(r)}=[E_{i,j-1}^{(r-s_{j-1,j})},E_{j-1}^{(s_{j-1,j}+1)}],\qquad F_{j,i}^{(r)}=[F_{j-1}^{(s_{j,j-1}+1)},F_{j-1,i}^{(r-s_{j,j-1})}].$$

These are [BK, Section 2.1, (2.7)–(2.18), and Section 2.2, (2.21)–(2.22)], with the negative root written in matrix-row order here. Two filtrations are fixed on it: the **canonical
filtration**, in which each generator of upper index $r$ has degree $r$, and
the **loop filtration**, in which it has degree $r-1$; their associated
graded algebras are different (the canonical one is commutative polynomial,
the loop one is a current algebra).

For the pyramid $\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$ with conjugate
$q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$ ([[def-a-type-a-nilpotent-pyramid-good-grading-and-whittaker-character]])
the relevant shift matrix is $s_{i,j}=p_j-p_i$ for $i\le j$ and $s_{i,j}=0$
for $i\ge j$, and the **type-A finite W-algebra** is the quotient
$$W(\lambda)=Y_n(\sigma)/\bigl(D_1^{(r)},\ r>p_1\bigr)$$
of $Y_n(\sigma)$ by the two-sided ideal generated by the higher modes of
$D_1$ beyond $p_1$.

Write the Gauss decomposition $T(u)=F(u)D(u)E(u)$ of the generating matrix,
with $T(u)=\sum_{r\ge0}T_{i,j}^{(r)}u^{-r}$, $T_{i,j}^{(0)}=\delta_{i,j}$, and
**no** additional factor $u^{s_{i,j}}$: the coefficient of $u^{-r}$ is the
mode $T_{i,j}^{(r)}$. Its modes satisfy $T_{i,j}^{(r)}=0$ for
$0<r\le s_{i,j}$, and in the finite quotient also $T_{i,j}^{(r)}=0$ for
$r>S_{i,j}:=s_{i,j}+p_{\min(i,j)}$, so the finite quotient has the PBW basis
of ordered monomials
$$T_{i,j}^{(r)},\qquad s_{i,j}<r\le S_{i,j}.$$
The auxiliary signed path polynomials used in the source to construct the
Gauss generators are not all identified with these shifted $T$-modes; the root
of $T_{i,j}^{(r)}$ is the weight $\varepsilon_i-\varepsilon_j$, and the
surviving modes have loop leading term $(-1)^{r-1}e_{i,j;r-1}$ in the
centralizer basis of the pyramid.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The abstract RTT/shifted Drinfeld data, the original pyramid shift, and the local well-definedness constructions of [F3].

1.1 **Ranges and shift arithmetic.** The monotone shift identities hold by telescoping $p_k-p_i=(p_j-p_i)+(p_k-p_j)$ on increasing indices and by zero lower shifts on decreasing indices. The adjacent positive generators have threshold $s_{i,i+1}$, the adjacent negative generators threshold $s_{i+1,i}$, and their higher-root commutator recursions give respectively $s_{i,j}$ and $s_{j,i}$. Thus for the asymmetric original pyramid an upper coefficient begins after $p_j-p_i$ whereas its lower counterpart begins at mode $1$; these are distinct ranges. The formal Gauss coefficients are computed by triangular inversion with diagonal constant term $1$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 **Infinite filtrations.** The RTT relation lowers canonical degree under a commutator, and its degree-$r+s-2$ loop part is the current Lie bracket. The actual ordered-product evaluation and Gauss Jacobian in [F3] prove independence of the ordered root-mode words, while the defining relations give spanning with both degree assignments. Therefore the canonical associated graded is polynomial and the loop associated graded is the enveloping algebra of the shifted current Lie subalgebra. Their distinction follows from their respective multiplication, rather than filtered-element independence alone. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 **Finite quotient and actual reduction.** By [F3], the actual signed path images satisfy the shifted coefficient relations and $D_1^{(r)}=0$ for $r>p_1$. The coefficient reductions give finite spanning words in the abstract quotient. Their images are independent invariant monomials, whose weighted count equals every filtered dimension of the independently constructed whole reduction. Hence the quotient maps isomorphically to that reduction. The finite $T$ coefficient induction gives zero below the shift and above $S_{i,j}=s_{i,j}+p_{\min(i,j)}$, and the finite Gauss-to-$T$ coordinate change gives the ordered surviving $T$-monomial basis. This uses finite spanning and independent reduction images; restriction of an infinite PBW basis to a quotient would not prove independence. Only $D_1$ is directly truncated: higher diagonal Gauss coefficients remain polynomial expressions. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 **Weights and actual loop symbols.** The path of canonical degree $r$ with $k$ matrix factors has good degree at most $r-k$, so only its single-factor part contributes in loop degree $r-1$. It is $(-1)^{r-1}e_{i,j;r-1}$, of row weight $\varepsilon_i-\varepsilon_j$. The ambient homogeneous centralizer basis and enveloping PBW in [F3] make these symbols and their ordered products independent, establishing the finite loop filtration. Auxiliary paths use their declared cut and sign conventions and are not automatically all the shifted $T$ coefficients. For $p=(1,2)$ the upper threshold is $s_{1,2}=1$, so the first upper coefficient is $T_{1,2}^{(2)}$ with symbol $-e_{1,2;1}$; the corresponding lower threshold is $s_{2,1}=0$. This verifies the unrescaled coefficient convention and the asymmetric range. [F1, F3, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

references.title: Jonathan Brundan and Alexander Kleshchev, Representations of shifted Yangians and finite W-algebras, Mem. Amer. Math. Soc. 196 (2008), no. 918 (complete 109-page arXiv memoir)
references.locator: Chapter 2, printed pp. 9-22: the shifted Yangian Y_n(sigma), its generators and shift matrix, the canonical and loop filtrations, the Gauss decomposition T=FDE, the PBW theorem, and the finite truncation; Chapter 3, printed pp. 24-33: the quotient presentation of W(pi) by the modes D_1^(r), r>p_1, and the vanishing ranges of the T modes.

references.title: Jonathan Brundan and Alexander Kleshchev, Shifted Yangians and finite W-algebras, arXiv:math/0407012 (49 pp.); Parabolic presentations of the Yangian Y(gl_n), arXiv:math/0407011 (28 pp.)
references.locator: Sections 2-6 of the first paper: shifted Drinfeld and parabolic relations, Gauss factorization T=FDE and the coefficient proofs; Sections 2-6 of the second: RTT identities and the evaluation proof of the ordered PBW basis. The finite-W index ranges are expanded in owner-category-o-batch17-affine-yangian-proof.md Sections 3-5 and owner-category-o-batch17-finite-w-matrix-proof.md Sections 1-2.

items.title: Gan-Ginzburg and Skryabin inputs for the type-A pyramid good grading
items.statement:
Keep the pyramid data $(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak p,\mathfrak h,\mathfrak m,e,\chi)$
of [[def-a-type-a-nilpotent-pyramid-good-grading-and-whittaker-character]] and
the finite W-algebra $W(\lambda)$, the bimodule $Q_\chi=U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$
and the Whittaker category of
[[def-the-type-a-finite-w-algebra-and-whittaker-category]]. Double the pyramid
grading by declaring the degree of $e_{i,j}$ to be
$2(\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i))$; then $e$ has degree $2$ and the
degree $-1$ part of $\mathfrak g$ is zero. Let
$\mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r>0,\ r\ \mathrm{even}}\mathfrak g_{-r}$ in the doubled
grading (the strictly negative even part), carrying the character $\chi$. Then:

1. There is a homogeneous transverse complement
   $S=e+\ker(\operatorname{ad} f)$ for a suitable $f\in\mathfrak g$, and the
   conjugation map $M_{\mathrm{unip}}\times S\to e+\mathfrak m^\perp$,
   $(u,s)\mapsto usu^{-1}$, is a polynomial isomorphism; the Kazhdan
   associated graded of $Q_\chi$ is $\mathbb C[M_{\mathrm{unip}}]\otimes\mathbb C[S]$
   and $\operatorname{gr}W(\lambda)=\mathbb C[S]$.
2. Assuming the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]], for every $W(\lambda)$-module $X$, the twisted $\mathfrak m$-cohomology of
   $Q_\chi\otimes_{W(\lambda)}X$ vanishes in positive degree and its degree-zero
   part is $X$.
3. Every nonzero module on which all $x-\chi(x)$, $x\in\mathfrak m$, act
   locally nilpotently has a nonzero simultaneous invariant vector; in
   particular $\mathrm{Wh}(M)=0$ implies $M=0$ for $M$ in the Whittaker
   category.

These assertions use the doubled good grading; no nondegenerate alternating
form on the original degree $-1$ space is asserted.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The pyramid data, the doubled grading $\deg e_{i,j}=2(\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i))$, the subspaces $\mathfrak m,\mathfrak p$ in the doubled grading, the ideals $I_\chi$, $U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ and the bimodule $Q_\chi$, and the finite W-algebra $W(\lambda)$. For assertion (2), assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]; assertions (1) and (3) do not require it.

[F1] In the doubled grading the only nonzero even degrees occur, $e$ has degree $2$, $\mathfrak p=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}\mathfrak g_r$ and $\mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r<0}\mathfrak g_r$ consist of even degrees only, and the string computation of the pyramid gives $\mathfrak m^\perp=[\mathfrak m,e]\oplus\ker(\operatorname{ad} f)$ for an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple $(e,h,f)$ adapted to the grading ([[def-a-type-a-nilpotent-pyramid-good-grading-and-whittaker-character]], [[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]).

[F2] Chevalley-Eilenberg theory: the $\mathfrak m$-cohomology of a module is computed by the Chevalley-Eilenberg complex, $H^0$ is the space of invariants, and a short exact sequence of $\mathfrak m$-modules gives a long exact cohomology sequence ([[def-chevalley-eilenberg-cochains]], [[def-chevalley-eilenberg-differential]], [[def-lie-algebra-cohomology]], [[prop-zero-th-lie-algebra-cohomology-is-invariants]], [[thm-long-exact-sequence-in-lie-algebra-cohomology]]).

[F3] PBW orders the nonnegative-degree algebra $\mathfrak p$ before $\mathfrak m$ and replaces the rightmost $\mathfrak m$ generators by their character in $Q_\chi$. The resulting Kazhdan filtration is exhaustive, separated and bounded below; its symbols are polynomial functions on $e+\mathfrak m^\perp$. The twisted $\mathfrak m$ action has as symbol the infinitesimal conjugation action. These assertions follow by reordering the enveloping-algebra relations and the character quotient; no transverse Clifford factor is present in this even grading ([[def-the-type-a-finite-w-algebra-and-whittaker-category]], [[def-universal-enveloping-algebra]], [[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]).


[F4] The Axiom of Choice permits the right-module splittings used in the bounded augmented complex for assertion (2) ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). No choice principle is invoked in assertions (1) and (3).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The doubled grading, the transverse slice $S$ and the bimodule $Q_\chi$; assume AC for assertion (2), as in [F4].

1.1 **Positive-weight transverse product.** Choose the usual rowwise $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ triple. On $\operatorname{Hom}(R_b,R_a)$ the strings have highest $h$-weight $p_a+p_b-2k$, $1\le k\le\min(p_a,p_b)$. Since the pyramid grading element differs from $h$ by row scalars, their highest and lowest grading weights are $2(p_b-k)\ge0$ and $-2(p_a-k)\le0$. Thus the negative-degree part is injected by $\operatorname{ad}e$ and gives the direct-sum complement of [F1]. The differential of $\alpha(u,z)=uzu^{-1}$ at $(1,e)$ is $(x,y)\mapsto[x,e]+y$, an isomorphism. Use weight $-H$ on $\mathfrak m$ and weight $2-H$ on the translated slice and target coordinates; these are positive. In homogeneous coordinates of increasing weight, each component of $\alpha$ is an invertible linear block in the variables of that weight plus a polynomial in lower-weight variables. Successive substitution constructs its polynomial inverse. In particular derivative invertibility alone is not being used as a global inverse theorem. [F1, F3, construct, algebra]

1.2 **Detection.** The shifted operators $x-\chi(x)$ form a representation of the nilpotent Lie algebra $\mathfrak m$, because $\chi$ kills brackets. A nonzero central element has a nonzero kernel on any nonzero locally nilpotent module: apply its largest nonvanishing power to a nonzero vector. That kernel is stable, and the quotient Lie algebra acts on it with the same local nilpotence. Induction on $\dim\mathfrak m$ therefore gives a common nonzero invariant. The case $\mathfrak m=0$ is immediate. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 **The actual graded complex.** PBW and [F3] give $\operatorname{gr}Q_\chi=\mathbb C[e+\mathfrak m^\perp]$, with no additional symbol factor. Step 1.1 identifies this with $\mathbb C[M_{\mathrm{unip}}]\otimes\mathbb C[S]$. Infinitesimal conjugation acts by invariant vector fields on the first factor and trivially on the slice factor. Giving the exterior dual of a grading-degree $-2r$ vector weight $2r$ makes the twisted Chevalley–Eilenberg differential filtration preserving. Its graded complex is the polynomial de Rham complex of $M_{\mathrm{unip}}$, tensored with $\mathbb C[S]$: invariant vector fields trivialize the tangent bundle and the bracket terms are precisely the de Rham differential. Polynomial exponential coordinates identify this unipotent group with affine space. On a polynomial form of positive total degree $t$, $t^{-1}\iota_{\mathrm{Euler}}$ is a contracting homotopy; constants are the only surviving degree-zero classes. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **Filtered lifting and right freeness.** A positive-degree cocycle in the actual complex has a graded leading term which is a boundary by step 2.1. Lift that boundary and subtract it, strictly lowering the integer filtration degree; boundedness below terminates this process. The same procedure lifts every graded invariant, using vanishing of graded degree-one cohomology to remove its differential. Hence $H^{>0}(\mathfrak m,Q_\chi)=0$ and $\operatorname{gr}W=\mathbb C[S]$, since $H^0(\mathfrak m,Q_\chi)=W$ by the defining invariant realization. Using the fixed PBW vector-space identification $U(\mathfrak p)\to Q_\chi$, take homogeneous coordinate representatives in $U(\mathfrak p)$ and form their ordered products there before projecting to $Q_\chi$. This never multiplies abstract classes in a left-ideal quotient. Their projected ordered monomials, acted on by the right $W$ bimodule action, span $Q_\chi$ by finite descending leading-term subtraction. A finite relation among them would give a relation between distinct monomials over $\operatorname{gr}W$; independence of polynomial monomials rules this out. Thus $Q_\chi$ is right $W$-free. All statements include the independent scalar coordinate of $\mathfrak{gl}_N$. [F2, F3, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **Transfer to every module without graded-flatness assumptions.** The finite augmented cochain complex $0\to W\to C^0\to\cdots\to C^{\dim\mathfrak m}\to0$, where $C^j=Q_\chi\otimes\bigwedge^j\mathfrak m^*$, is exact by step 3.1 and is a complex of right $W$-modules. Its differentials are right $W$-linear because the right action commutes with the twisted left $\mathfrak m$ action. Each term is right $W$-free. Starting at the last term, split each surjection onto the already-projective boundary module; descending induction makes every boundary projective and splits every short exact sequence, including $W\hookrightarrow C^0$. These splittings supply a right $W$-linear contraction of the augmented complex. Tensor the contraction with an arbitrary left $W$-module $X$. This remains a contraction, and the resulting complex is exactly the twisted Chevalley–Eilenberg complex of $Q_\chi\otimes_W X$. Consequently its positive cohomology vanishes and its degree-zero cohomology is $X$ via $x\mapsto1_\chi\otimes x$. No filtration or flatness of $X$ is assumed. The splittings use exactly [F4]. [F2, F4, step 3.1, choose, construct, algebra]

5.1 The preceding steps prove the three assertions with the doubled even grading. In particular there is no degree $-1$ symplectic or Clifford contribution. If $e=0$, then $\mathfrak m=0$ and the product, augmentation and all cohomology identities reduce to their degree-zero identities. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Remarks

- The role of the doubling is to put the contracting $\mathbb C^\times$-weights in even degrees so that the Kazhdan symbols are the coordinate functions of the unipotent group; the loop filtration of the finite W-algebra is a different filtration and is treated separately later on this page.

- The detection statement is the categorical form of Skryabin's theorem used to identify Whittaker vectors: for $M$ in the Whittaker category, $M\mapsto\mathrm{Wh}(M)$ loses nothing.

references.title: Wee Liang Gan and Victor Ginzburg, Quantization of Slodowy slices, Int. Math. Res. Not. 2002, no. 5, 243-255 (complete 10-page arXiv article)
references.locator: Sections 2, 4 and 5, printed pp. 2-8: the Slodowy slice, the contracting action, the decomposition gr Q = C[N] tensor gr H, and the vanishing of the positive-degree part of the twisted cohomology; Section 6, Theorem 6.1: Skryabin's equivalence and the detection statement Wh(E)=0 implies E=0.

references.title: Jonathan Brundan, Simon M. Goodwin and Alexander Kleshchev, Highest weight theory for finite W-algebras, Int. Math. Res. Not. 2008, no. 15 (complete 38-page arXiv article)

items.title: Ordered monomial PBW basis for the shifted Yangian
items.statement:
For any fixed order on the family $D_i^{(r)}$ ($r\ge1$),
$E_{i,j}^{(r)}$ ($i<j$, $r>s_{i,j}$), and $F_{j,i}^{(r)}$ ($i<j$, $r>s_{j,i}$),
with each root mode included once, their ordered monomials form a $\mathbb C$-basis of $Y_n(\sigma)$. Its canonical associated graded algebra is the polynomial
algebra on the corresponding symbols, while its loop associated graded algebra
is the universal enveloping algebra of the current algebra
$\mathfrak{gl}_n[t](\sigma)$; the two graded algebras are different and
non-isomorphic in general. In the finite quotient $W(\lambda)$ the ordered
monomials in the finite Gauss range
$$s_{i,j}<r\le s_{i,j}+p_{\min(i,j)}$$
form a basis, and the commutative Kazhdan/canonical associated graded and the
noncommutative loop associated graded are distinct. Equivalently, the finite
$T$-coefficients with $s_{i,j}<r\le S_{i,j}$ form an ordered PBW basis, where
$r$ is the unshifted coefficient index of $T=FDE$, not a reindexed value.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The shifted Yangian generators and the finite quotient $W(\lambda)$.

1.1 **RTT spanning and the actual coproduct.** In the unshifted RTT algebra the commutator of modes $r,s$ has canonical degree at most $r+s-1$, so induction on total degree and the number of unordered pairs rewrites every word into ordered monomials. Matrix-unit brackets verify RTT for $L_a(u)=I+E^{(a)}/u$ in the $a$th factor of $U(\mathfrak{gl}_n)^{\otimes l}$. Multiplication of RTT matrices with commuting coefficient algebras preserves RTT: moving the two middle commuting tensor factors past each other allows the first RTT identity, then the second. Thus the iterated evaluation map is $T(u)\mapsto L_1(u)\cdots L_l(u)$. More generally shifted evaluation points give the ordered product $\prod_{a=1}^l(I+E^{(a)}/(u-c_a))$, in increasing factor order. Its $u^{-r}$ coefficient when all $c_a=0$ is $\sum_{a_1<\cdots<a_r}E^{(a_1)}\cdots E^{(a_r)}$, homogeneous of enveloping PBW degree $r$. [F1, F2, algebra, construct]

1.2 We first prove invariance of the actual path generators for both column arrangements, independently of generation. For a box a write c(a) for its column, $\rho_c=n-\sum_{d\ge c}q_d$ and $\widetilde E_{ab}=(-1)^{c(b)-c(a)}(E_{ab}+\delta_{ab}\rho_{c(a)})$. The negative PBW projection $\operatorname{pr}:U(\mathfrak g)=U(\mathfrak p)U(\mathfrak m)\to U(\mathfrak p)$ applies χ to the right factor. Its elementary rules are $\operatorname{pr}(ZB)=\chi(Z)B+\operatorname{pr}([Z,B])$ and $\operatorname{pr}(BZ)=B\chi(Z)$ for a negative matrix unit Z and a p-factor B. The bracket is $[\widetilde E_{ab},\widetilde E_{hk}]=\delta_{bh}(\widetilde E_{ak}-\delta_{ak}\rho_{c(a)})-\delta_{ak}(\widetilde E_{hb}-\delta_{hb}\rho_{c(b)})$, and $\chi(\widetilde E_{ab})=-\delta_{\operatorname{row}(a),\operatorname{row}(b)}$ at adjacent negative columns, zero at greater distance. Define $P_{ij;x}^{(r)}$ as the sum of products $E_{a_1b_1}\cdots E_{a_sb_s}$ with total degree $\sum(c(b_t)-c(a_t)+1)=r$, p-factors, shared intervening rows, starting/ending rows i,j, strict forward joins when the intervening row exceeds x and weak reverse joins otherwise, and sign $(-1)^{r-s}$ times one minus for every intervening row at most x. Its $\eta_{\rm tail}$ image replaces each factor by $E_{ab}+\delta_{ab}\rho_{c(a)}$. Equivalently, in the $\widetilde E$ factors its only external sign is one minus for every intervening row at most x, since their product already contributes $(-1)^{r-s}$. Invariance means $\operatorname{pr}([z,\eta_{\rm tail}(P)])=0$. If an element B is invariant, then $(z-\chi(z))B=B(z-\chi(z))+[z,B]$ proves $U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi B\subseteq U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$; hence invariant elements form a subalgebra, and products, commutators and coefficients of inverse series with identity constant are invariant. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 The local Gan–Ginzburg supplier is stated for the original left-justified diagram; we derive the reflected version by an actual graded Lie isomorphism. Let f reflect boxes, $\tau(E_{ab})=E'_{f(b),f(a)}$ reverse products, and let S on the reflected space be diagonal with $S_{bb}=(-1)^{\operatorname{col}'(b)}$. The linear map $\phi(x)=S(-\tau(x))S^{-1}$ is a Lie isomorphism, because $[\tau(x),\tau(y)]=-\tau([x,y])$. It preserves grading degrees, p and m, and the trace pairing. The diagonal-conjugation sign on every positive adjacent arrow is −1, so $\phi(e)=e'$ and $\chi'\phi=\chi$. It extends to an ALGEBRA isomorphism of enveloping algebras and takes $U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ to $U(\mathfrak g')I_{\chi'}$. Thus it takes the entire untwisted left reduction $A=\eta_{\rm tail}(W)$ to $A'$: each defining commutator condition is equivalent under φ. The chart map is the explicit algebra isomorphism $\beta=\eta_{\rm tail}'^{-1}\phi\eta_{\rm tail}:W\to W'$. Scalar translations have smaller positive Kazhdan degree, so $\operatorname{gr}\beta=\operatorname{gr}\phi$. The doubled good grading, sl2 triple, trace-orthogonal slice and transverse product transport under φ. Consequently the proved original polynomial-slice and cohomological statements imply the reflected statements in its actual grading, including the homogeneous coordinate weights. The polynomial-slice part used here is choice-free; for consumers assuming AC as in the cohomological supplier, its left Skryabin quotient, local-nilpotence category, invariant space and equivalence maps also transport first through φ and then through β. This uses the original proved local supplier without enlarging its stated domain, and does not assert that a transpose subalgebra is the whole reflected reduction or that two chart twists act equally on a fixed module. [F1, F2, F3, construct, algebra]

1.4 **Index and inverse sign in the abstract quotient.** Write $A_i(u)=D_i(u)^{-1}=\sum_{t\ge0}A_i^{(t)}u^{-t}$, so $A_i^{(0)}=1$, while the defining relation uses $\widetilde D_i(u)=-A_i(u)$ with constant $-1$. Thus $[E_i^{(a)},F_i^{(b)}]=-D_{i+1}^{(a+b-1)}-\sum_{t=1}^{a+b-1}A_i^{(t)}D_{i+1}^{(a+b-1-t)}$. Put $i=c-1$, $u=s_{c-1,c}$, $v=s_{c,c-1}$, $a=r-v$, $b=v+1$. Then $a+b-1=r$ and $D_c^{(r)}=-\sum_{t=1}^rA_{c-1}^{(t)}D_c^{(r-t)}-[E_{c-1}^{(r-v)},F_{c-1}^{(v+1)}]$. We use this only for $r>p_c=p_{c-1}+u+v$, so $a>p_{c-1}+u$ is an allowed but HIGH E mode, to be eliminated before the diagonal formula is used. Also $A_i^{(r)}=-\sum_{t=1}^rD_i^{(t)}A_i^{(r-t)}$, giving polynomial inverse coefficients with the same canonical degree bound. This derives the sign and indices, rather than treating a negative inverse as a positive one. [F1, algebra]

2.1 **Product Jacobian and independence.** Let $l$ be at least the largest coefficient index in a proposed relation. In the commutative symbol algebra of $U(\mathfrak{gl}_n)^{\otimes l}$ write $P_r(X_1,\ldots,X_l)=\sum_{a_1<\cdots<a_r}X_{a_1}\cdots X_{a_r}$. At $X_a=h_aI$, with nonzero pairwise distinct $h_a$, the differential on every matrix entry is $dP_r=\sum_a e_{r-1}(h_1,\ldots,\widehat{h_a},\ldots,h_l)dX_a$. The column coefficient polynomials $\prod_{b\ne a}(1+h_bz)$ are linearly independent, since evaluating at $z=-1/h_c$ leaves only column $c$, with a nonzero value. Hence the Jacobian is invertible. A polynomial relation of minimal total degree, differentiated and multiplied by the inverse Jacobian over the rational function field, makes each of its partial derivatives a lower-degree relation; minimality and characteristic zero force the relation to be constant and zero. Thus the coordinates $P_{r,ij}$, $1\le r\le l$, are algebraically independent. A highest weighted-degree part of an enveloping relation among their ordered lifts would contradict this polynomial independence by [F2]. This proves RTT PBW for all modes. The $h_a$ are scalar-matrix points in the symbol space, independently of spectral evaluation parameters. [F2, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

2.2 Group equal row lengths into the minimal admissible parabolic blocks ν, with final nonempty block m of size t. D/E/F below are its actual Gauss path coefficients. Deleting the last column embeds the smaller shifted matrix units into the current ones; on unshifted diagonal units this compensates the rho difference by a scalar translation, and on negative units it preserves χ. A dot denotes the smaller coefficients. With final column A, preceding column B, $L_{kj}=\widetilde E_{(A,k),(A,j)}$ and $C_{hj}=\widetilde E_{(B,h),(A,j)}$, the right end recursions, for any fixed bottom row h, are $D_{a;ij}^{(r)}=\dot D_{a;ij}^{(r)}+\delta_{a,m}(\sum_k\dot D_{a;ik}^{(r-1)}L_{kj}+[\dot D_{a;ih}^{(r-1)},C_{hj}])$, $E_{a;ij}^{(r)}=\dot E_{a;ij}^{(r)}+\delta_{a,m-1}(\sum_k\dot E_{a;ik}^{(r-1)}L_{kj}+[\dot E_{a;ih}^{(r-1)},C_{hj}])$, and $F_{a;ij}^{(r)}=\dot F_{a;ij}^{(r)}$. The E boundary formula is used for r>1. Deleting the FIRST column of the reflected arrangement has the ordinary embedding on the remaining shifted factors. With first column A, next B, $L_{ik}=\widetilde E_{(A,i),(A,k)}$ and $C_{ih}=\widetilde E_{(A,i),(B,h)}$, its LEFT recursions are $D_{a;ij}^{(r)}=\dot D_{a;ij}^{(r)}+\delta_{a,m}(\sum_kL_{ik}\dot D_{a;kj}^{(r-1)}+[C_{ih},\dot D_{a;hj}^{(r-1)}])$, $E_{a;ij}^{(r)}=\dot E_{a;ij}^{(r)}$, and $F_{a;ij}^{(r)}=\dot F_{a;ij}^{(r)}+\delta_{a,m-1}(\sum_kL_{ik}\dot F_{a;kj}^{(r-1)}+[C_{ih},\dot F_{a;hj}^{(r-1)}])$, with r>1 in the F boundary formula. To verify these identities, cut each path at its final or initial visit to the added column. Paths missing that column give the dotted coefficient; paths ending or starting in its block give the product sum. For a crossing path the two neighboring cut positions at the common bottom row h have opposite signs and give the two orders in the commutator; further visits pair by moving to the neighboring cut. The identical cut rule in a changed row interval proves the Gauss identities: paths without an intermediate visit occur once; paths with such a visit have the two neighboring cuts with opposite sign. Thus these are identities for the actual Gauss coefficients. In particular LEFT deletion corrects F and leaves E unchanged; it does not use the interchanged E/F display in the source. [F1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

2.3 **Finite spanning: earlier blocks and boundary E/F.** In the abstract quotient by $D_1^{(r)}$, $r>p_1$, let $\Omega_c$ contain D modes $1\le a\le c$, $1\le r\le p_a$, E roots $a<b\le c$, $s_{ab}<r\le s_{ab}+p_a$, and F roots $a<b\le c$, $s_{ba}<r\le s_{ba}+p_a$; let $B_c$ be their algebra. Induct on c to show every allowed mode with endpoints at most c belongs to $B_c$ with total canonical degree at most its index. The case c=1 is the imposed truncation, including $p_1=0$. For the inductive step put $u=s_{c-1,c}$ and $v=s_{c,c-1}$. For $r>u+p_{c-1}$, the D–E relation gives $E_{c-1}^{(r)}=[D_{c-1}^{(r-u)},E_{c-1}^{(u+1)}]-\sum_{t=1}^{r-u-1}D_{c-1}^{(t)}E_{c-1}^{(r-t)}$. Replace every earlier D by its block-inductive finite expression and expand its commutator by Leibniz. The bracket of an earlier finite diagonal mode of index a with the lowest boundary E gives terms $D^{(t)}E_{c-1}^{(a+u-t)}$ with $a\le p_{c-1}$ in the only nonzero diagonal block, hence new E indices at most $u+p_{c-1}$. An earlier finite root $E_{b,c-1}^{(a)}$ gives $E_{b,c}^{(a+u)}$ and any block-refinement split terms, all with $a+u\le s_{b,c-1}+p_b+u=s_{b,c}+p_b$. Earlier negative roots and earlier positive roots without endpoint $c-1$ commute with the lowest boundary E. Thus the expanded commutator is in $B_c$. In the sum $u+1\le r-t<r$, so induction on r reduces those E modes; all products have degree at most r. The reversed D–F relation and reversed product orders give the same argument with boundary bound $v+p_{c-1}$. [F1, step 1.4, algebra]

3.1 **Gauss and shifted PBW.** Coefficientwise formal inversion and $T=FDE$ give mutually inverse polynomial changes between RTT and Gauss coordinates: the Gauss mode of index $r$ equals the corresponding RTT coordinate plus expressions in smaller mode indices of total canonical degree $r$. Consequently the canonical symbols of all Gauss root modes are a polynomial coordinate system. The shifted Drinfeld relations straighten shifted root-mode words, with lower canonical-degree commutator corrections; the adjacent root commutator definitions and Serre relations perform the higher-root straightening. Their RTT images have the same Gauss symbols in the allowed shifted ranges. Those symbols form an independent subset of the polynomial coordinate system, so these spanning words are independent and the shifted presentation embeds. Thus its canonical associated graded is precisely the polynomial algebra on its allowed root symbols. This argument concerns the untruncated algebra; it does not infer independence after quotienting. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Induct on the number of columns, deleting the last column in the original left-justified diagram and the first in the reflected diagram. A one-column diagram has no negative algebra, so every mode is invariant. Empty rows have only formal constants and zero positive coefficients. All earlier D blocks, all nonboundary E/F blocks, and F in right deletion or E in left deletion are unchanged by step 2.2. Their path monomials have no forbidden preceding-bottom target in right deletion, or following-bottom source in left deletion; commuting a new negative into such a monomial produces a negative unit of greater column distance with zero χ, and moving it to the right keeps this absent endpoint. Thus their projected brackets vanish. Induction supplies old-negative invariance of every dotted coefficient. The old negative algebra commutes with L and C in step 2.2, so its character ideal is preserved by those factors, proving old-negative invariance of the changed coefficients. The complete negative Lie algebra is generated by the old one and the new adjacent-column matrices: brackets through a row present in intervening bottom rows produce each longer negative matrix. Jacobi and the normalizer identity in step 1.2 propagate invariance from these generators. Only the new adjacent matrices need be checked below. [step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra]

3.3 **Higher roots and the final diagonal elimination.** For $b<c-1$, the defining root recursions are $E_{b,c}^{(r)}=[E_{b,c-1}^{(r-u)},E_{c-1}^{(u+1)}]$ and $F_{c,b}^{(r)}=[F_{c-1}^{(v+1)},F_{c-1,b}^{(r-v)}]$. Reduce the earlier endpoint factors by the c−1 hypothesis; the same Leibniz bounds in step 2.3 place every new root in $B_c$, including high modes, using the finite allowed new roots in $\Omega_c$. Now use step 1.4 for $D_c^{(r)}$, $r>p_c$. Every inverse earlier coefficient is in $B_{c-1}$ and every $D_c^{(r-t)}$ has smaller index, so induction on r treats its sum. First replace the upper $E_{c-1}^{(r-v)}$ by the finite expression just constructed, then expand the bracket with the lowest boundary F. Earlier D/F factors give bounded new F roots and earlier factors; earlier E factors commute with that boundary F. A finite new E root starting at c−1 has index $a\le u+p_{c-1}$, so its E–F convolution has only $D_c$ indices at most $a+v\le p_c$. A new E root starting at b<c−1 gives earlier-endpoint roots and earlier factors, reduced by the block hypothesis, and cannot create a high $D_c$ mode. Thus this commutator uses only $D_c$ indices at most $p_c$, and the induction closes with the asserted degree control. In particular higher diagonal modes are polynomial expressions, not zero modes. [F1, step 1.4, step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 The changed D^(1) is a sum of the row-pair diagonal-column blocks; its two adjacent-column projected commutators cancel. Let the neighboring column have height u≥t, with b=u−t shorter rows and cutoff x=n−t. In RIGHT deletion put $z=\widetilde E_{(A,f),(B,g)}$, f bottom and g arbitrary. In D^(2), and in boundary E^(2) when the shift is1, the single bridge contributes scalar $-u\delta_{gi}\delta_{fj}$. The bottom plus paths $\sum_kB_{ik}A_{kj}$ contribute $+t\delta_{gi}\delta_{fj}$ and matrix terms $-\delta_{gi}A_{fj}+\delta_{fj}B_{ig}$ for g bottom. The shorter minus paths in B contribute $+b\delta_{gi}\delta_{fj}$ and $+\delta_{fj}B_{ig}$ for g shorter. Moving their negative factor through the following block yields one additional χ correction for each shorter row; this is the scalar b term. The single bridge gives the negative of all the matrix terms, and $-u+t+b=0$. In LEFT deletion put $z=\widetilde E_{(B,f),(A,g)}$, f arbitrary and g bottom. The bridge scalar is $-t\delta_{gi}\delta_{fj}$; bottom plus paths $\sum_kA_{ik}B_{kj}$ give $+t\delta_{gi}\delta_{fj}$ and $-\delta_{gi}B_{fj}+\delta_{fj}A_{ig}$ for f bottom. Shorter minus paths $-\sum_hB_{ih}B_{hj}$ give $-\delta_{gi}B_{fj}$ for f shorter and NO scalar: the extra negative χ involves a shorter row h and bottom row g. The bridge has the opposite matrix terms. Therefore $-t+t=0$ and all matrices cancel, for D^(2) and boundary F^(2). Paths outside these adjacent columns have zero projection by the support argument in step 3.2. This proves the exact jump-one base cases in both actual LEFT reductions. [step 1.2, step 2.2, step 3.2, algebra]

4.2 For a larger boundary shift, or a rectangle, the first two end columns have equal height t. A double dot deletes both and $K_{s;ij}=\ddot D_{m;ij}^{(s)}$; replacing K with the corresponding boundary $\ddot E$ in RIGHT deletion or $\ddot F$ in LEFT deletion gives the same calculation. In RIGHT deletion call the last positions C,B,A, and write $B_{ck}=\widetilde E_{(B,c),(B,k)}$, $A_{kj}=\widetilde E_{(A,k),(A,j)}$, $C_{hk}=\widetilde E_{(C,h),(B,k)}$, $J_{cj}=\widetilde E_{(B,c),(A,j)}$ and $H_{hj}=\widetilde E_{(C,h),(A,j)}$. Twice expanding step 2.2 expresses the changed r-mode as the sum of eight groups $A_0=K_{r;ij}$, $B_0=\sum_cK_{r-1;ic}B_{cj}$, $C_0=[K_{r-1;ih},C_{hj}]$, $D_0=\sum_kK_{r-1;ik}A_{kj}$, $E_0=\sum_{k,c}K_{r-2;ic}B_{ck}A_{kj}$, $F_0=\sum_k[K_{r-2;ih},C_{hk}]A_{kj}$, $G_0=\sum_cK_{r-2;ic}J_{cj}$, $H_0=[K_{r-2;ih},H_{hj}]$. For $z=\widetilde E_{(A,f),(B,g)}$ their projected brackets, in that order, are $0,-\delta_{fj}K_{r-1;ig},0,+\delta_{fj}K_{r-1;ig},R,S,-R,-S$, where $R=t\delta_{fj}K_{r-2;ig}-K_{r-2;ig}A_{fj}+\delta_{fj}\sum_cK_{r-2;ic}B_{cg}$ and $S=\delta_{fj}[K_{r-2;ih},C_{hg}]$. The bracket in step 1.2 proves this table by moving each negative factor to the RIGHT. The t summation rows give the scalar in R; the bridge J gives its opposite because $\rho_A-\rho_B=t$. K lies in the twice-deleted p and commutes with z. The eight expressions cancel for EVERY r>1. [step 1.2, step 2.2, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 At a RIGHT jump-one boundary, for a fixed earlier-block row g and r>1 the coefficient recursions in U(p) are $D_{m;ij}^{(r+1)}=[F_{m-1;ig}^{(2)},E_{m-1;gj}^{(r)}]+\sum_{s=0}^r\widetilde D_{m-1;gg}^{(r+1-s)}D_{m;ij}^{(s)}$ and $E_{m-1;ij}^{(r+1)}=[D_{m-1;ig}^{(2)},E_{m-1;gj}^{(r)}]-\sum_fD_{m-1;if}^{(1)}E_{m-1;fj}^{(r)}$. Here $\widetilde D(u)=-D(u)^{-1}$, with order-zero coefficient −I. The corresponding LEFT identities are $D_{m;ij}^{(r+1)}=[F_{m-1;ig}^{(r)},E_{m-1;gj}^{(2)}]+\sum_{s=0}^rD_{m;ij}^{(s)}\widetilde D_{m-1;gg}^{(r+1-s)}$ and $F_{m-1;ij}^{(r+1)}=[F_{m-1;ig}^{(r)},D_{m-1;gj}^{(2)}]-\sum_fF_{m-1;if}^{(r)}D_{m-1;fj}^{(1)}$. These are algebraic coefficient identities, independent of invariance and generation. Expanding the E identity by the right end recursion gives $\dot E^{(r+1)}+\sum\dot D^{(1)}\dot E^{(r)}$, its product with L, and its commutator with C; collecting with step 2.2 gives $E^{(r+1)}+\sum D^{(1)}E^{(r)}$. The left F expansion instead gives $\dot F^{(r+1)}+\sum\dot F^{(r)}\dot D^{(1)}$, its LEFT product with L and $[C,\,\cdot\,]$, which collect to $F^{(r+1)}+\sum F^{(r)}D^{(1)}$. The unchanged earlier D^(2) has no boundary endpoint and commutes with L,C. Expanding the boundary E–F bracket similarly gives the D identity: the coefficient convolution $D\widetilde D=-I$ cancels paired split paths with opposite cut signs, leaving the changed D coefficient. Thus the recursions hold in both product orders. Every earlier D/inverse-D coefficient and the unaffected E or F coefficient is invariant by step 3.2; the changed base coefficients are invariant by step 4.1. Since the sum uses s≤r, induction on r proves invariance of ALL changed jump-one modes. [step 1.2, step 2.2, step 3.2, step 4.1, algebra]

5.2 The REFLECTED calculation is a direct LEFT-ideal calculation, not an anti-map reversal of step 4.2. Call its first positions A,B,C, and write $L_{ik}=\widetilde E_{(A,i),(A,k)}$, $B_{kc}=\widetilde E_{(B,k),(B,c)}$, $C_{kh}=\widetilde E_{(B,k),(C,h)}$, $J_{ic}=\widetilde E_{(A,i),(B,c)}$, $H_{ih}=\widetilde E_{(A,i),(C,h)}$. The eight groups are $A_0=K_{r;ij}$, $B_0=\sum_kB_{ik}K_{r-1;kj}$, $C_0=[C_{ih},K_{r-1;hj}]$, $D_0=\sum_kL_{ik}K_{r-1;kj}$, $E_0=\sum_{k,c}L_{ik}B_{kc}K_{r-2;cj}$, $F_0=\sum_kL_{ik}[C_{kh},K_{r-2;hj}]$, $G_0=\sum_cJ_{ic}K_{r-2;cj}$, $H_0=[H_{ih},K_{r-2;hj}]$. For $z=\widetilde E_{(B,f),(A,g)}$ their projected brackets are $0,+\delta_{ig}K_{r-1;fj},0,-\delta_{ig}K_{r-1;fj},R',S',-R',-S'$, with $R'=t\delta_{ig}K_{r-2;fj}-\delta_{ig}\sum_cB_{fc}K_{r-2;cj}+L_{ig}K_{r-2;fj}$ and $S'=-\delta_{ig}[C_{fh},K_{r-2;hj}]$. For example $[z,L_{ik}]=\delta_{gi}\widetilde E_{(B,f),(A,k)}$, and moving this negative through B gives $-\delta_{fk}B_{kc}+\delta_{fc}$; summing k gives the t term. The other part of the product bracket gives the L term. The bridge J has the opposite matrix terms and scalar $\rho_A-\rho_B=-t$; the F/H terms cancel because $[z,H_{ih}]=\delta_{gi}C_{fh}$ and z commutes with K. Thus every group is accounted for and cancels in the reflected LEFT reduction for EVERY r>1. If there are only two columns, K has only its formal constant coefficients and terms involving the third column vanish, so the same table applies. [step 1.2, step 2.2, step 3.2, algebra]

6.1 Steps 3.2, 4.1, 5.1, 4.2 and 5.2 cover every allowed parabolic D/E/F mode for the original and reflected arrangements. Refining a minimal block is its formal Gauss decomposition: coefficients of its inverse and resulting factors are polynomials in its previous coefficients, hence invariant by step 1.2. This gives all ordinary simple modes; higher-root commutator definitions give all higher roots. Therefore the actual untwisted-chart images $P_{ii;i-1}^{(r)},P_{i,i+1;i}^{(r)},P_{i+1,i;i}^{(r)}$ and all their higher-root polynomials belong to their actual left reductions. This conclusion covers the infinite allowed mode families and does not rely on finite generation, finite truncation or a reflected W identification. [step 1.2, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 4.2, step 5.2, algebra]

7.1 **Finite Levi Jacobian.** Project $U(\mathfrak p)$ to its column Levi enveloping algebra and take canonical symbols. At its diagonal point $X_c=h_cI$, let $Q_i(z)=\prod_{c\le p_i}(1+h_cz)$. The diagonal D first variations are $z\prod_{a\le p_i,a\ne c}(1+h_az)$. For $i<j$, set $m=p_i$, $M=p_j$. A first variation in a common column $c\le m$ has just one off-diagonal factor. Summing the same-column negative-cut repeats and the strictly increasing positive-cut visits in the path formula gives $dE_{ij}(z)=z\prod_{a=m+1}^M(1+h_az)/(1+h_cz)$ and $dF_{ji}(z)=z/(1+h_cz)$ on that entry. These are identities for the allowed coefficient derivatives, not an identification of excluded low product coefficients with shifted generators. Their coefficients in modes $M-m+k$ and $k$, $1\le k\le m$, are respectively $(-h_c)^{k-1}\prod_{a=m+1}^M(h_a-h_c)$ and $(-h_c)^{k-1}$. For higher roots, the canonical symbol of the adjacent root commutator is the Levi Lie–Poisson bracket. At $X_c=h_cI$ this Poisson tensor is zero, so the differential of a bracket uses only the two first differentials and the differential of the Poisson tensor. With $i<k<j$ and $p_k=t$, the coefficients from $E_{ik}^{(r-s_{kj})}$ and $E_{kj}^{(s_{kj}+1)}$ multiply to $(-h_c)^{a-1}\prod_{m<b\le t}(h_b-h_c)\prod_{t<b\le M}(h_b-h_c)$ when $r=M-m+a$, since $\{X_{c,ik},X_{c,kj}\}=X_{c,ij}$. For F the reversed recursion uses $\{X_{c,jk},X_{c,ki}\}=X_{c,ji}$, with coefficients one and $(-h_c)^{r-1}$. Thus induction gives the displayed first variations for all higher roots as well. Choose the $h_c$ nonzero and pairwise distinct. Each row-pair block is Vandermonde with nonzero column factors; each diagonal block is the elementary-symmetric Jacobian from step 2.1. Different row pairs use disjoint entry variables, so the full Jacobian has rank $\sum_{ij}\min(p_i,p_j)$. The corresponding finite symbols are algebraically independent by step 2.1's differentiation argument. Reflection reverses column order and interchanges E and F, giving the same invertible blocks with transposed shifts. Empty rows contribute zero-sized blocks. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 **The whole reduction is generated.** Write $\mathcal W$ for the entire quantum Hamiltonian reduction, before any identification with a Yangian quotient. By [F3] its homogeneous Hilbert series is $H(t)=\prod_{i,j}\prod_{r=s_{ij}+1}^{s_{ij}+\min(p_i,p_j)}(1-t^r)^{-1}$. Each weight is positive, so every coefficient is finite. Step 6.1 places every ordered finite-generator monomial of total degree at most $d$ inside $F_d^K\mathcal W$. Step 7.1 and enveloping PBW make these monomials independent: a highest-degree relation after Levi projection would give a polynomial relation among the independent symbols. Their number is exactly $\sum_{k\le d}[t^k]H(t)$, which is also $\dim F_d^K\mathcal W$ by [F3] for the original pair and step 1.3 for the reflected pair. Thus their span equals $F_d^K\mathcal W$ for every $d$. Exhaustivity proves generation of the entire reduction and its ordered filtered basis, and also injectivity of the Levi projection on that entire algebra. The same homogeneous dimension equality proves full generation for the reflected reduction using its own allowed modes and transposed shifts. This uses the Gan–Ginzburg slice theorem independently of W-PBW, not just generic independence in a restricted subalgebra. [F2, F3, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 1.3, algebra]

9.1 **Relations, finite order and the whole-algebra identification.** The end path identities prove the shifted coefficient relations and the $D_1$ cutoff on the invariant representatives. One can check them after Levi projection, now injective on the entire reduction by step 8.1: the right end images are $D_a^{(r)}\mapsto\dot D_a^{(r)}+\delta_{a,m}\sum_k\dot D_{a;ik}^{(r-1)}L_{kj}$, $E_a^{(r)}\mapsto\dot E_a^{(r)}+\delta_{a,m-1}\sum_k\dot E_{a;ik}^{(r-1)}L_{kj}$, and $F_a^{(r)}\mapsto\dot F_a^{(r)}$; the left versions place L before the dotted coefficients and correct F instead. Substitute these finite coefficient expressions in each D–D, D–E, D–F, E–F, equal-root and adjacent-root relation. Terms with no L give the smaller relation. Terms with one L give the smaller D-weight relation; terms with two L use $[L_{ij},L_{hk}]=\delta_{jh}L_{ik}-\delta_{ki}L_{hj}$. The inverse-D convolution cancels paired split coefficients, and the adjacent triple relations group into those same terms and the matrix Jacobi identity. Hence the relations hold by column induction, starting with matrix-unit brackets at one column; injectivity lifts them back to the actual reduction. For D1 the cutoff row interval is empty, so every join is strictly forward; a path beginning and ending in row1 satisfies $r=\sum(c(b_t)-c(a_t)+1)\le c(b_s)-c(a_1)+1\le p_1$. Thus the smallest-row path has no coefficient above $p_1$, giving the actual $D_1$ cutoff in either arrangement. There is therefore a homomorphism from the abstract truncated quotient onto the invariant-generated whole algebra. Steps 2.3 and 3.3 give finite spanning; commutator swapping lowers canonical degree, so induction on that degree and the number of unordered pairs straightens these finite expressions into ordered $\Omega_n$ monomials. Their images are the independent ordered reduction basis of step 8.1, so the homomorphism is injective as well. This proves the quotient presentation and the finite Gauss PBW basis without restricting an infinite basis through a quotient. [F1, F2, step 2.2, step 6.1, step 8.1, step 2.3, step 3.3, algebra]

9.2 The full generator theorem just proved for BOTH arrangements now identifies the original head/right model. With the reflected-box anti-map τ from step 1.3, send a path $(a_1,b_1),\ldots,(a_s,b_s)$ to $(f(b_s),f(a_s)),\ldots,(f(b_1),f(a_1))$. Each displacement is unchanged. A reversed join compares $l+1-c(a_{k+1})$ with $l+1-c(b_k)$, so its strict-forward or weak-reverse rule is exactly the original one; its row is $\operatorname{row}(a_{k+1})=\operatorname{row}(b_k)$, preserving its sign. Total degree, number of factors and total sign are identical; the product order is precisely τ's reversal. This involutive bijection proves $\tau(P_{ij;x}^{(r)})=P_{ji;x}^{\prime(r)}$ for ALL i,j,x and modes r, including the diagonal constants at r=0. In particular τ exchanges simple E/F images and fixes the corresponding D images, transposing the shift matrix and preserving mode number. Since these explicit images generate each WHOLE reduction by step 8.1, both inclusions give $\tau(W)=W'$, rather than only the image of a path subalgebra. [step 6.1, step 1.3, step 8.1, construct, algebra]

10.1 The preceding construction applies to both directional shift matrices, using the corresponding left or right end formulas in step 9.1. Thus it proves the full finite quotient basis, equality with the whole reduction, and strict canonical/Kazhdan filtration in both arrangements. Its degree-r homogeneous basis is the monomial basis counted by the exact slice Hilbert series, and the projection used for the relation check is injective on the entire reduction. These are the prerequisites for the original right-normalizer identification below. [step 1.3, step 8.1, step 9.1, algebra]

10.2 **Actual original prefix coefficient identity.** Let $\lambda_m$ be the first m columns of the decreasing-column pyramid, $I=I_{m-1}:U(\mathfrak g_{m-1})\hookrightarrow U(\mathfrak g_m)$ the ordinary UNSHIFTED box embedding, and $b_a(j)$ the box in row j and column a when it exists. Put negative-index coefficients zero and $T_{ij}^{(0)}=\delta_{ij}$. The original coefficient recursion, for r>0, is $T_{ij}^{(r)}(\lambda_m)=I(T_{ij}^{(r)})-\sum_{h\le n-q_m,\ s_{hj}\le r}I(T_{ih}^{(r-s_{hj})})I(T_{hj}^{(s_{hj})})+\sum_{h>n-q_m}I(T_{ih}^{(r-1)})E_{b_m(h),b_m(j)}-[I(T_{ij}^{(r-1)}),E_{b_{m-1}(j),b_m(j)}]$, where coefficients inside I belong to $\lambda_{m-1}$ and shifts in the sum belong to $\lambda_m$. The final THREE terms are omitted for $j\le n-q_m$, and a nonexistent box omits its term. To derive the identity before any cutoff is known, apply the right end identities to the last Gauss block in the ordinary chart. D has its smaller D plus its last-column Levi product and minus its previous-to-last bridge commutator; E has the same two corrections and starts with the smaller $\bar E$. The precise smaller-block subtraction is $\bar E_{a,b}(u)=E_{a,b}(u)-\sum_{c=a}^{b-1}E_{a,c}(u)E_{c,b}^{(\dot s_{cb}+1)}u^{-\dot s_{cb}-1}$, all in the smaller diagram. For a shorter block c and last block b, $\dot s_{cb}+1=s_{cb}$. Insert these expressions into $T_{ij}(u)=\sum(F_{c,a}(u)D_c(u)E_{c,b}(u))_{ij}$. Unchanged terms give the first embedded T; the $\bar E$ subtractions group by shorter terminal row h into the product with split $(r-s_{hj},s_{hj})$; the L products group into the Levi sum. Leibniz groups the common bridge into the displayed single commutator. Higher-root end identities follow by their adjacent recursion; its earlier-block factor has no terminal bridge endpoint, so its bracket with that bridge is zero. This proves the prefix identity itself and retains its actual coefficient index. [F1, step 2.2, step 9.1, algebra, construct]

11.1 **Loop symbols and the two graded algebras.** In the unshifted RTT relation the top loop-degree commutator is the current matrix-unit bracket; terms with two positive-index factors have smaller loop degree. Gauss multiplication changes a mode of index $r$ by products of at least two factors of total canonical index $r$, hence smaller loop degree than $r-1$. Taking the shifted root relations gives the same brackets with allowed current modes $e_{ij}t^a$, $a\ge s_{ij}$; shift additivity makes their span a Lie subalgebra. The ordered basis of step 3.1 is a filtered basis also for intrinsic loop degree, because loop straightening never raises total degree and independence of the full ordered words rules out a lower-degree expression. Current PBW uses only finite-dimensional PBW: any proposed relation uses finitely many modes, and a jet quotient with larger cutoff preserves those basis vectors and makes their enveloping monomials independent. Hence the loop associated graded is $U(\mathfrak{gl}_n[t](\sigma))$. Canonical degree instead gave a commutative polynomial algebra. For the finite reduction the Kazhdan associated graded is the commutative slice algebra from step 8.1, while the leading single-factor terms of the finite generators lie in the actual centralizer $\mathfrak g^e\subseteq\mathfrak p$; the next theorem identifies the loop graded algebra by ambient enveloping PBW. Noncommutativity distinguishes the two graded algebras whenever the corresponding Lie algebra is nonabelian. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.1, step 8.1, step 10.1, algebra]

11.2 **Every coefficient above the bound is zero.** For the original decreasing-column diagram $S_{ij}=s_{ij}+\min(p_i,p_j)=p_j$ for EVERY ordered row pair. Induct on the column count m using step 10.2; the one-column T has no coefficient above one directly. An empty row contributes only a diagonal constant. If $j\le n-q_m$, its row length is unchanged on removal, so the only embedded T term vanishes for $r>p_j$ by induction. If j is a bottom row, $p_j=m$, and the first embedded T vanishes for $r>m$ because its smaller target-row length is m−1. In each shorter-row product, $p_h$ is unchanged and $s_{hj}=m-p_h$, so $r-s_{hj}>p_h=S_{ih}(\lambda_{m-1})$ for ANY i, killing its first factor. In the Levi sum every h has smaller row length m−1, and $r-1>m-1=S_{ih}(\lambda_{m-1})$ kills its coefficient. The same inequality kills the T coefficient inside the final commutator. This covers every term, including the boundary $r=m+1$, and proves $T_{ij}^{(r)}=0$ for $r>S_{ij}$. The lower zero range $0<r\le s_{ij}$ follows coefficientwise from FDE and shift additivity. No truncation fact was assumed to prove itself. [F1, step 10.2, algebra]

12.1 **Finite T coordinates and loop symbols.** Coefficientwise FDE and Gauss inversion are weighted triangular in the original index r: the mode equals its corresponding Gauss coordinate plus products of smaller mode indices of total canonical degree r. The finite Gauss eliminations from steps 2.3 and 3.3 and the actual cutoff in step 11.2 close both inversions on exactly the finite set. Thus these finite canonical symbols are another polynomial coordinate system, and the ordered finite T monomials have the same filtered basis as the Gauss monomials in step 9.1, in any prescribed order. A signed path term with k factors and coefficient index r has ambient good degree at most r−k; scalar replacements lower it further. Only its single-factor part contributes in degree r−1, giving $(-1)^{r-1}\sum_{\operatorname{row}(a)=i,\operatorname{row}(b)=j,\ c(b)-c(a)=r-1}E_{ab}=(-1)^{r-1}e_{ij;r-1}$. Products introduced by Gauss inversion have at least two factors and smaller good degree. This proves the symbol dictionary with the existing coefficient index and no spectral rescaling. [F1, step 3.3, step 9.1, step 11.2, algebra]

12.2 Put $\eta_{\rm head}(E_{ab})=E_{ab}+\delta_{ab}(n-\sum_{d\le c(a)}q_d)$. This and ηtail are algebra automorphisms: a matrix bracket can have diagonal part only from $E_{ab},E_{ba}\in\mathfrak p$, which forces equal columns and equal diagonal shifts, so the scalar functional kills the commutator; the negative scalar translation is the inverse. Reflection gives $\sum_{d\ge c'(f(a))}q'_d=\sum_{d\le c(a)}q_d$, hence $\tau\eta_{\rm head}=\eta'_{\rm tail}\tau$. Also $\tau(\mathfrak m)=\mathfrak m'$, $\chi'\tau=\chi$ by the trace calculation, and $\tau(I_\chi U(\mathfrak g))=U(\mathfrak g')I_{\chi'}$, since τ reverses products and sends each shifted negative generator to its reflected one. Therefore $\tau([\eta_{\rm head}(u),x])=[\tau(x),\eta'_{\rm tail}(\tau(u))]$. Bijectivity shows that u satisfies the ORIGINAL head/right condition exactly when τ(u) belongs to the reflected LEFT reduction. Step 9.2 identifies its inverse image with the original W, proving BOTH inclusions in $W=\{u:[\eta_{\rm head}(u),\mathfrak m]\subseteq I_\chi U(\mathfrak g)\}$. The induced Gauss transpose also satisfies $\tau(T_{ij}^{(r)})=T_{ji}^{\prime(r)}$: apply the coefficientwise reversed FDE factors and their Gauss cut identities. Thus step 11.2 gives the reflected upper cutoff $r>S_{ji}=S_{ij}^{\prime}$, with the same finite triangular T basis. This proves right invariance for every original shifted generator, higher-root mode and product, beyond the numerical identity $\eta_{\rm head}-\eta_{\rm tail}=-\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak m}\operatorname{ad}$. [step 9.2, algebra]

13.1 Write $J_L=U(\mathfrak g)I_\chi$ and $J_R=I_\chi U(\mathfrak g)$. The identities $(x-\chi(x))\eta_{\rm tail}(w)=\eta_{\rm tail}(w)(x-\chi(x))+[x,\eta_{\rm tail}(w)]$ and $\eta_{\rm head}(w)(x-\chi(x))=(x-\chi(x))\eta_{\rm head}(w)+[\eta_{\rm head}(w),x]$ prove $J_L\eta_{\rm tail}(w)\subseteq J_L$ and $\eta_{\rm head}(w)J_R\subseteq J_R$ for every w∈W. Thus $Q_L=U(\mathfrak g)/J_L$ has its actual right action $\overline a\cdot w=\overline{a\eta_{\rm tail}(w)}$, and $Q_R=U(\mathfrak g)/J_R$ its actual left action $w\cdot\overline a=\overline{\eta_{\rm head}(w)a}$, commuting with the respective enveloping actions by associativity. These are module quotients, not quotient rings. Right Whittaker vectors act by $v\cdot w=v\eta_{\rm head}(w)$ because they annihilate J_R. Turning a right U(g)-module into a left reflected module by $a'v=v\tau^{-1}(a')$ identifies its right Whittaker space and W action with the reflected left ones, using $\tau^{-1}\eta'_{\rm tail}\tau=\eta_{\rm head}$. For consumers assuming AC, transporting their proved left Skryabin equivalence through the reflected Lie isomorphism in step 1.3 and then this anti-map gives the right equivalence with inverse $-\otimes_WQ_R$; that conditional categorical assertion is separate from the choice-free algebra identity. Every action is the explicit original or reflected chart action; no equality of different twists on an arbitrary fixed representation is assumed. [step 1.3, step 12.2, algebra] ∎
